practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Name the two hormones produced by the pancreas that control blood glucose concentration.
practice_questions.marks: Insulin and glucagon (1 mark — both needed).

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens in the body when blood glucose concentration rises above the normal level.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The pancreas releases insulin into the blood (1); insulin causes body cells to take up glucose and the liver to convert excess glucose to glycogen, lowering blood glucose back to normal (1). Emerging: Vague — e.g. 'insulin is made and lowers glucose' without identifying where glucose goes.

practice_questions.text: Explain how vasoconstriction helps the body conserve heat when core temperature drops.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Blood vessels near the skin surface narrow (vasoconstrict) (1); less warm blood flows close to the skin surface (1); so less heat is lost to the surroundings by radiation, conserving heat in the body's core (1). Secure: Two points logically linked. Developing: States 'vessels narrow so less blood goes to skin' but does not explain the effect on heat loss. Emerging: Confused — e.g. 'vasoconstriction makes blood hotter'.

practice_questions.text: A student measures their blood glucose at four time points: fasting (5.0 mmol/L), 30 min after a meal (8.4 mmol/L), 60 min after a meal (6.9 mmol/L) and 120 min after a meal (5.1 mmol/L). Calculate the percentage decrease in blood glucose between 30 min and 120 min. Show your working and give your answer to 1 decimal place.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Decrease = 8.4 − 5.1 = 3.3 mmol/L (1); percentage decrease = (3.3 ÷ 8.4) × 100 (1) = 39.28...% (1); rounded correctly to 39.3% (1). Penalise missing % symbol or incorrect rounding. Secure: Correct method with arithmetic error in one step (max 3 marks).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a person with Type 1 diabetes requires insulin injections but a person with Type 2 diabetes may be able to manage their condition without injections.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: In Type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys insulin-producing beta cells so no insulin is produced; without injections, blood glucose cannot be controlled (1). In Type 2 diabetes, the pancreas may still produce insulin but body cells are resistant to it (1); lifestyle changes such as diet and exercise can reduce insulin resistance and improve glucose uptake without the need for injections (1). Secure: Two of the three points. Developing: Distinguishes the two types but does not explain why injections are only needed in Type 1. Emerging: Confuses the two types.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of negative feedback in maintaining blood glucose homeostasis. In your answer, explain what would happen if negative feedback mechanisms failed, with reference to diabetes as an example.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Negative feedback ensures that any deviation from the set point (normal blood glucose) triggers a corrective response that brings glucose back to normal — preventing it from rising too high (hyperglycaemia) or falling too low (hypoglycaemia), both of which are dangerous. Without insulin (as in Type 1 diabetes), blood glucose can rise after eating and cells are deprived of glucose for respiration, leading to fatigue, organ damage and, if untreated, diabetic ketoacidosis. Without glucagon (Higher Tier), blood glucose could fall dangerously, impairing brain function since the brain relies almost entirely on glucose. The fact that two opposing hormones (insulin and glucagon) are involved makes the system more responsive and precise than a single-hormone system. A clear evaluative conclusion on why negative feedback is essential for survival. Secure: Four well-made points. Developing: Two points, limited evaluation. Emerging: One relevant point.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the arrangement and movement of particles in a liquid?
A) Regular arrangement, vibrate in fixed positions
B) Irregular arrangement, move randomly at high speed, far apart
C) Irregular arrangement, close together, slide past each other
D) Regular arrangement, far apart, strong attractive forces
practice_questions.marks: C) Irregular arrangement, close together, slide past each other [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the name given to the change of state when a substance converts directly from a solid to a gas.
practice_questions.marks: Sublimation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the temperature changes when a pure substance is heated from solid to gas, and explain what happens at the melting point.
practice_questions.marks: Temperature rises as the solid heats up, stays constant (flat section) at the melting point as the solid converts to liquid, then rises again as the liquid heats up [1 mark]; at the melting point, energy supplied is used to break forces between particles rather than raising the kinetic energy of particles, so temperature stays constant [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a physical change and a chemical change. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: A physical change does not produce any new substances and is reversible [1 mark]; a chemical change produces one or more new substances with different properties and is usually irreversible [1 mark]; example of physical: melting ice, dissolving salt (accept any valid physical change); example of chemical: burning wood, cooking food, rusting iron [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A student heats a sample of an impure solid and measures its temperature over time. She notices that the substance begins to melt at 45°C and finishes melting at 52°C.
A pure sample of the same substance melts at exactly 48°C.
Explain these observations using your knowledge of the particle model.
practice_questions.marks:
A pure substance has particles of one type, all held together by forces of the same strength, so all particles overcome these forces at the same temperature, giving a sharp melting point [1 mark]
Impurities disrupt the regular arrangement of particles in the solid [1 mark]; different impurity particles are held by forces of different strengths [1 mark]; so different particles overcome these forces at different temperatures, giving a range of melting temperatures rather than a single sharp point [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain two limitations of the simple particle model in describing the behaviour of matter.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two limitations clearly stated with precise explanation of what each prevents the model from explaining; examples given; accurate scientific language throughout.
Secure: Two limitations described with partial explanation; some scientific terminology.
Developing: One clear limitation or two vague ones; limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement about the model without specific limitations.

Limitations may include:
(1) The model treats all particles as identical solid spheres of the same size, ignoring that different atoms, molecules and ions have different sizes and masses. This means the model cannot explain why different substances have different properties such as different melting and boiling points.
(2) The model does not represent the forces of attraction between particles. In reality it is these forces (bonds and intermolecular forces) that hold matter together and determine state. The model appears to show particles simply touching or repelling.
(3) In gas diagrams, particles are usually shown much closer together than they actually are — gas particles are typically very much further apart than solid or liquid particles.
Top band answers name two limitations, explain what each one fails to account for, and link it to a property the model cannot explain.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the number of moles of solute in 250 cm³ of a 0.200 mol/dm³ sodium chloride solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Converts 250 cm³ to 0.250 dm³; applies n = c × V = 0.200 × 0.250 = 0.0500 mol; units stated.
Secure: Correct method with a minor arithmetic or unit error.
Developing: Sets up n = c × V but fails to convert cm³ to dm³, giving answer of 50 mol.
Emerging: Recalls the equation but cannot substitute or convert units.

practice_questions.text: Determine the concentration of a solution containing 0.0400 mol of potassium hydroxide dissolved in 500 cm³ of solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Converts 500 cm³ to 0.500 dm³; c = n ÷ V = 0.0400 ÷ 0.500 = 0.0800 mol/dm³; units correct.
Secure: Correct calculation with one minor error (e.g. rounding or unit omission).
Developing: Divides but uses 500 rather than 0.500, giving 0.0000800 mol/dm³.
Emerging: Equation recalled but not applied correctly.

practice_questions.text: In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide (KOH) solution requires 22.5 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid to reach the end point. The equation is: KOH + HCl → KCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the KOH solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: V(HCl) = 0.0225 dm³; n(HCl) = 0.100 × 0.0225 = 0.00225 mol; mole ratio 1:1 so n(KOH) = 0.00225 mol; V(KOH) = 0.0250 dm³; c(KOH) = 0.00225 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0900 mol/dm³. Units throughout.
Secure: All steps shown, one arithmetic or conversion error.
Developing: Moles of HCl correct; ratio applied; final division step missing or incorrect.
Emerging: Concentration equation recalled but steps not completed.

practice_questions.text: A student carries out four titrations. Their results are: 18.40 cm³, 18.35 cm³, 17.80 cm³ and 18.30 cm³. Explain which results they should use to calculate the mean, and calculate the mean titre.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that 17.80 cm³ is anomalous (more than 0.10 cm³ from the others) and should be excluded; mean of concordant results = (18.40 + 18.35 + 18.30) ÷ 3 = 18.35 cm³. Explanation of concordant results included.
Secure: Identifies anomalous result and calculates correct mean with minor rounding error.
Developing: Excludes anomalous result but does not explain why; mean calculation attempted.
Emerging: Some attempt to identify the outlier or calculate a mean, but not both.

practice_questions.text: Sulfuric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. 15.0 cm³ of 0.0500 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄ reacts completely with 25.0 cm³ of NaOH solution. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: n(H₂SO₄) = 0.0500 × 0.0150 = 7.50 × 10⁻⁴ mol; mole ratio 1:2 so n(NaOH) = 1.50 × 10⁻³ mol; c(NaOH) = 1.50 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0600 mol/dm³; all units present.
Secure: Correct mole ratio applied; one arithmetic or conversion error.
Developing: Moles of acid calculated correctly; 1:2 ratio not applied (treats as 1:1).
Emerging: First step only — converts volume.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a student would carry out an accurate acid–alkali titration in the laboratory, including the steps taken to ensure a reliable result.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes using a pipette to measure a fixed volume of alkali into a conical flask; adding indicator (names one — e.g. phenolphthalein or methyl orange); filling burette with acid and noting initial reading; adding acid slowly, swirling the flask; adding drop by drop near the end point; noting the colour change at end point; recording final burette reading; calculating titre; repeating to obtain concordant results (within 0.10 cm³); calculating the mean of concordant titres. Clear, ordered description.
Secure: Most steps present; one or two missing (e.g. swirling or slow addition near end point).
Developing: Key apparatus named; end point identified; repeatability not mentioned.
Emerging: Some relevant apparatus named; partial procedure with significant omissions.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly defines oxidation?
A) Gain of electrons or loss of oxygen
B) Loss of electrons or gain of oxygen
C) Gain of electrons or gain of oxygen
D) Loss of electrons or loss of oxygen
practice_questions.marks: B) Loss of electrons or gain of oxygen [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the products formed when zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid.
practice_questions.marks: Zinc chloride (ZnCl₂) and hydrogen (H₂). [1 mark — both required]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid.
practice_questions.marks: A strong acid fully dissociates (ionises) into ions in water [1 mark]; a concentrated acid has a large amount (many moles) of acid dissolved per unit volume, regardless of how strongly it ionises [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: When magnesium is added to copper sulfate solution, a displacement reaction occurs. Explain why this reaction is also a redox reaction, identifying which species is oxidised and which is reduced.
practice_questions.marks: Magnesium is more reactive than copper (higher in the reactivity series), so it displaces copper [1 mark]; magnesium is oxidised (it loses electrons / forms Mg²⁺ ions) [1 mark]; copper ions are reduced (they gain electrons / form Cu atoms) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
A student wants to make copper sulfate crystals by reacting copper oxide with sulfuric acid.

Write a word equation for this reaction and describe how the student would obtain pure crystals of copper sulfate from the resulting solution.
practice_questions.marks: Word equation: copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water [1 mark]; add excess copper oxide to warm sulfuric acid and stir until no more dissolves [1 mark]; filter to remove excess copper oxide [1 mark]; evaporate the filtrate slowly / heat gently to concentrate then allow to cool and crystallise [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Explain what happens during a neutralisation reaction between an acid and an alkali. In your answer, include:
• the ionic equation for the reaction
• why neutralisation is considered a redox reaction or not
• how you could use titration to produce a pure salt solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correct ionic equation (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O) with explanation that acid provides H⁺ ions and alkali provides OH⁻ ions; clear statement that neutralisation is NOT a redox reaction (no electron transfer, no change in oxidation state); detailed titration procedure including indicator, burette, end point detection, and repeat without indicator to obtain a pure solution; evaporation to produce crystals.
Secure: Correct ionic equation; neutralisation correctly identified as not redox with justification; titration procedure mostly correct.
Developing: Ionic equation present or partially correct; some titration steps described; redox point attempted.
Emerging: Basic statement that acid + alkali = salt + water; limited detail on titration or ionic equation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is found in a bacterial cell but NOT in an animal cell?
A) Mitochondria
B) Plasmids
C) Nucleus
D) Chloroplasts
practice_questions.marks:
B) Plasmids [1 mark]

Note: Plasmids are small rings of extra DNA found in prokaryotic cells such as bacteria. Animal cells never contain them. Bacterial cells also have no mitochondria, no true nucleus and no chloroplasts, and both cell types have a cell membrane.

practice_questions.text: State two sub-cellular structures found in plant cells but not in animal cells.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the following (1 mark for any two correct):
• Cell wall
• Chloroplasts
• Permanent vacuole
[1 mark for naming two correct structures]

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would prepare a light microscope slide of onion epidermis cells to view them under a microscope.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for any two of the following:
• Peel a thin layer of onion epidermis / place a thin sample on the slide
• Add a drop of stain (e.g. iodine solution) to make structures visible
• Lower a coverslip at 45° (at an angle) to avoid air bubbles
• Start on the lowest power objective lens before switching to higher magnification
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why electron microscopes have increased our understanding of cell biology compared with light microscopes.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Electron microscopes have a much higher resolution than light microscopes (1)
• This allows sub-cellular structures / organelles such as ribosomes or cristae to be seen in detail (1)
• Light microscopes cannot resolve structures smaller than approximately 200 nm, so these organelles could not be distinguished before (1)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A student looks at a cell under a microscope. The image of the cell is 45 mm wide. The actual width of the cell is 30 μm. Calculate the magnification used. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Magnification = image size ÷ real size (1)
45 mm = 45,000 μm (1)
Magnification = 45,000 ÷ 30 (1)
= ×1500 (1)
[4 marks — 1 for formula, 1 for unit conversion, 1 for substitution, 1 for correct answer with no units]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain the differences between eukaryotic cells and prokaryotic cells.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (award up to 6 marks for a well-structured response covering both description and explanation):
• Eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus surrounded by a nuclear membrane; prokaryotic cells have no nucleus — the DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm (1+1)
• Eukaryotic cells are generally larger and more complex than prokaryotic cells (1)
• Both types have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes (though prokaryotic ribosomes are smaller) (1)
• Prokaryotic cells may have plasmids — small rings of extra DNA; eukaryotic cells do not (generally) (1)
• Plant and animal cells are eukaryotic; bacteria are prokaryotic (1)

StudyVault Mastering: full comparison of both cell types with structural detail and function-linked explanations for all differences.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a longitudinal wave.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: a wave in which the vibrations/oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer/wave travel.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a compression and a rarefaction in a sound wave.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: a compression is a region where particles are pushed close together (high pressure). 1 mark: a rarefaction is a region where particles are spread further apart (low pressure).

practice_questions.text: A water wave has a frequency of 2.5 Hz and a wavelength of 0.4 m. Calculate the wave speed. Show your working and give the unit.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct equation v = f × λ. 1 mark: correct substitution v = 2.5 × 0.4. 1 mark: correct answer 1.0. 1 mark: correct unit m/s.

practice_questions.text: Explain why sound diffracts around a doorway but visible light does not.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that diffraction is greatest when gap width is similar to wavelength; states that sound has wavelengths similar in size to a doorway (tens of centimetres) whereas visible light has a much shorter wavelength (hundreds of nanometres), so light shows negligible diffraction through a doorway. Secure: states sound diffracts because its wavelength is similar to the gap; light does not because its wavelength is much smaller than the gap. Developing: states that the wavelength of sound is similar to the doorway but does not quantify or compare light's wavelength. Emerging: vague reference to wavelength without a comparison.

practice_questions.text: A wave travels from air into glass and bends towards the normal. What does this tell you about the wave's speed in glass compared to air?
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: The wave slows down in glass. Distractors: The wave speeds up in glass; The wave's frequency decreases; The wave's amplitude increases.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether a ripple tank is a suitable method for measuring the speed of water waves. Include limitations in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: describes method clearly (measure λ from wave pattern, record frequency from motor, apply v = fλ); evaluates limitations (parallax error reading wavelength from screen, water depth affects speed so must be kept constant, waves may not be perfectly planar near edges); concludes it is suitable with care. Secure: describes method and identifies at least two limitations. Developing: describes basic method but limitations are vague. Emerging: mentions ripple tank without explaining how measurements are taken.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes the particle arrangement in a liquid?
A) Particles in fixed positions, vibrating about those positions
B) Particles close together but able to flow past each other
C) Particles far apart, moving rapidly in random directions
D) Particles in a regular lattice with no movement
practice_questions.marks: B) Particles close together but able to flow past each other [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would measure the density of an irregularly shaped stone.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for: Measure the mass of the stone using a balance (1). Measure the volume using water displacement — submerge the stone in a measuring cylinder of water and record the rise in water level (volume of stone = rise in level) (1). Then calculate density = mass ÷ volume. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A steel ball has a mass of 390 g and a volume of 50 cm³. Calculate its density in g/cm³ and in kg/m³. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Correct equation stated: ρ = m/V (1). Correct substitution: ρ = 390 ÷ 50 (1). Correct answer in g/cm³: 7.8 g/cm³ (1). Correct conversion to kg/m³: 7800 kg/m³ (1). [4 marks — common error: dividing volume by mass, or failing to convert units]

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the particle model, why a gas has a much lower density than the same substance in its solid state.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In a solid, particles are closely and regularly packed, so a large mass is contained in a small volume, giving high density. In a gas, the same particles are very widely spaced (large distances between them) with negligible intermolecular forces, so the same mass occupies a much larger volume, giving very low density.
Secure: Particle spacing in each state described correctly with link to density.
Developing: States particles are far apart in gas and close in solid, but no link to mass/volume/density.
Emerging: States that gases are less dense than solids with no particle model explanation. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the pressure inside a sealed aerosol can increases if the can is placed near a heat source.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Heating the gas inside the can increases the kinetic energy of the gas particles; they move faster; collisions with the walls become more frequent and each collision exerts a greater force; the pressure inside the can therefore increases.
Secure: Faster particles and more frequent/forceful collisions described; linked to pressure increase.
Developing: States particles move faster when heated; link to pressure increase stated but not explained.
Emerging: States pressure increases when heated with no particle-level explanation. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) A diving bell is lowered to a depth of 40 m in sea water. The density of sea water is 1025 kg/m³ and g = 10 N/kg. Calculate the pressure due to the sea water at this depth. Show all steps.
practice_questions.marks: Correct equation: p = hρg (1). Correct substitution: p = 40 × 1025 × 10 (1). Correct answer: 410 000 Pa (or 4.1 × 10⁵ Pa) (1). Correct unit stated: Pa or pascals (1). [4 marks — Higher tier question; common errors: swapping h and ρ, omitting the unit]

practice_questions.text: Calculate the volume of gas produced, at RTP, when 0.25 mol of a gas is released in a reaction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States molar gas volume at RTP = 24 dm³/mol; volume = 0.25 × 24 = 6.0 dm³; units stated.
Secure: Correct calculation; minor unit error.
Developing: Uses 24 but does not state the principle; answer has no units.
Emerging: Recalls 24 but cannot set up the calculation.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the number of moles in 1200 cm³ of carbon dioxide gas at RTP.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Converts 1200 cm³ to 1.200 dm³; n = 1.200 ÷ 24 = 0.0500 mol; units correct.
Secure: Correct method; forgot to convert cm³ to dm³ (n = 1200 ÷ 24 = 50 mol — common error, penalise once).
Developing: Divides by 24 but does not convert volume.
Emerging: Attempts division but incorrect formula.

practice_questions.text: A reaction produces 4.20 g of a product. The maximum theoretical yield was 6.00 g. Calculate the percentage yield.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: percentage yield = (4.20 ÷ 6.00) × 100 = 70.0%; equation stated; values substituted correctly; answer expressed as percentage.
Secure: Correct answer with minor arithmetic error or percentage symbol missing.
Developing: Values correct but inverted (6.00 ÷ 4.20 × 100).
Emerging: Recalls the concept of yield but cannot apply equation.

practice_questions.text: The reaction for the production of ammonia is: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Explain why atom economy for this reaction is 100%.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that atom economy = Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all products × 100; notes there is only one product (NH₃) so all atoms from the reactants end up in the desired product; therefore atom economy = 100%.
Secure: Identifies single product and links to all atoms being in the desired product.
Developing: States atom economy is 100% because no by-products, without explaining what atom economy measures.
Emerging: States the reaction is efficient with no scientific explanation.

practice_questions.text: Iron(III) oxide is reduced with carbon: 2Fe₂O₃ + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for iron. [Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16, C = 12]
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mr of 4Fe = 4 × 56 = 224; Mr of 3CO₂ = 3 × (12 + 32) = 3 × 44 = 132; sum of all products = 224 + 132 = 356; atom economy = (224 ÷ 356) × 100 = 62.9% (3 s.f.); units (%) stated.
Secure: Correct method with one arithmetic error in Mr calculation.
Developing: Divides Mr(Fe) by Mr of reactants rather than all products.
Emerging: Mr of Fe calculated correctly but equation not applied.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a high atom economy is desirable in industrial chemistry, and why 100% percentage yield is not achievable in practice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: High atom economy: reduces waste (fewer by-products to dispose of), more efficient use of raw materials, lower environmental impact, more cost-effective. 100% yield impossible: reactions may be reversible and not go to completion; product is lost during purification/filtration/evaporation; side reactions may consume some reactant; product may remain in solution. Clear distinction between the two concepts maintained.
Secure: Both ideas addressed with at least two valid points each; clear scientific reasoning.
Developing: Atom economy or percentage yield addressed well; the other addressed briefly.
Emerging: One concept partially explained with limited detail.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the lock and key hypothesis?
A) The enzyme changes shape to fit the substrate
B) The substrate has a complementary shape to the enzyme's active site
C) Any substrate can bind to any enzyme active site
D) The active site is in the cytoplasm
practice_questions.marks: B) The substrate has a complementary shape to the enzyme's active site [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the base pairing rules in DNA.
practice_questions.marks: Adenine (A) pairs with thymine (T); cytosine (C) pairs with guanine (G) [1 mark — both pairs required]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to an enzyme when the temperature exceeds its optimum.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for:
• The enzyme is denatured (1)
• The active site changes shape permanently so the substrate can no longer fit / the enzyme can no longer catalyse the reaction (1)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why embryonic stem cells are considered more useful medically than adult stem cells, and why their use is controversial.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into any type of cell in the body (they are pluripotent), whereas adult stem cells can only produce a limited range of cell types (1)
• This makes embryonic stem cells potentially more useful for treating a wider range of diseases/conditions (1)
• Their use is controversial because the embryo is destroyed in the process, which some people consider morally wrong (1)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A student investigates the effect of pH on the activity of an enzyme. At pH 2 the enzyme takes 90 seconds to complete the reaction. At pH 7 it takes 30 seconds. Calculate the rate of reaction at pH 7 and compare it with the rate at pH 2. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Rate at pH 7 = 1 ÷ 30 = 0.033 s⁻¹ (to 2 s.f.) (1+1)
Rate at pH 2 = 1 ÷ 90 = 0.011 s⁻¹ (1)
Rate at pH 7 is approximately 3 times faster than at pH 2 / the enzyme has a higher rate at pH 7 (1)
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Describe the role of DNA in protein synthesis and explain why different proteins have different functions.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (up to 6 marks):
• DNA is a polymer with a double helix structure made of nucleotides with complementary base pairs (A–T, C–G) (1)
• The sequence of bases acts as a code — every three bases codes for a specific amino acid (triplet code) (1)
• In the nucleus, a section of DNA is used as a template to make mRNA (1)
• mRNA carries the code to ribosomes in the cytoplasm, where amino acids are assembled in the correct order (1)
• The sequence of amino acids determines the shape of the protein (1)
• Different sequences produce proteins with different shapes and therefore different functions — e.g. enzymes, antibodies, hormones (1)

StudyVault Mastering: all six points covered with precise terminology throughout.

practice_questions.text:
During electrolysis, which electrode do positive ions (cations) move towards?
A) The anode
B) The cathode
C) Both electrodes equally
D) Neither electrode
practice_questions.marks: B) The cathode [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the three products obtained from the electrolysis of brine.
practice_questions.marks: Hydrogen, chlorine, sodium hydroxide. [1 mark for all three correct]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens at the cathode and anode when molten aluminium oxide is electrolysed.
practice_questions.marks: Cathode: aluminium ions gain electrons / aluminium metal is deposited [1 mark]; Anode: oxide ions lose electrons / oxygen gas is released [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain why cryolite is mixed with aluminium oxide during the electrolysis process used to extract aluminium.
practice_questions.marks: Aluminium oxide has a very high melting point [1 mark]; cryolite (a mineral) dissolves the aluminium oxide, which lowers the melting point of the mixture significantly [1 mark]; this means less energy is needed to keep the electrolyte molten, reducing costs [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
A student electrolyses copper(II) sulfate solution using inert (carbon) electrodes.

(a) State the product formed at the cathode. [1 mark]
(b) State the product formed at the anode. [1 mark]
(c) (Higher tier) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode. [2 marks]
practice_questions.marks: (a) Copper (metal deposited) — copper is less reactive than hydrogen [1 mark]; (b) Oxygen — no halide ion present, so OH⁻ ions are discharged [1 mark]; (c) Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu — correct formula [1 mark], correctly balanced with electrons [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Explain the industrial importance of the electrolysis of brine, describing the products formed at each electrode and their uses. Include the half-equations for the reactions at the cathode and anode.

Higher Tier candidates should include the half-equations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three products correctly identified (hydrogen at cathode, chlorine at anode, sodium hydroxide remaining); explanation that sodium is too reactive to be deposited, so H⁺ ions are discharged at cathode instead; chloride ions preferentially discharged at anode over OH⁻ ions; industrial uses for all three products stated (e.g. chlorine for bleach and PVC; hydrogen for fuel; NaOH for soap and paper); correct half-equations written and balanced.
Secure: Three products identified with at least two uses; competition at electrodes explained; half-equations present but may have minor errors.
Developing: Two products correctly identified; some uses stated; half-equations attempted.
Emerging: One product identified; limited explanation of electrode processes.

practice_questions.text: Name the EM wave with the longest wavelength.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: radio waves.

practice_questions.text: Describe one use of infrared radiation and explain why infrared is suitable for that use.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct named use (e.g. remote control, thermal imaging, fibre optic communication, night-vision). 1 mark: relevant explanation linking a property of IR to the use (e.g. IR is absorbed by warm objects so thermal cameras detect temperature differences; or IR travels along optical fibres for data transmission).

practice_questions.text: A microwave has a frequency of 2.4 GHz. Calculate its wavelength. (Speed of EM waves = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.)
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct equation λ = c / f. 1 mark: correct conversion 2.4 GHz = 2.4 × 10⁹ Hz. 1 mark: correct substitution λ = 3 × 10⁸ ÷ (2.4 × 10⁹). 1 mark: correct answer 0.125 m (accept 1.25 × 10⁻¹ m), correct unit.

practice_questions.text: Explain why X-rays can be used to image bones but are not used to image soft tissue such as muscle.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that X-rays are transmitted through soft tissue but absorbed by denser bone; the difference in transmission creates contrast on the image plate/detector; bone shows up as a lighter region because fewer X-rays pass through. Secure: states X-rays pass through soft tissue but not bone, producing a shadow image. Developing: states X-rays pass through the body and show bones without explaining why there is contrast. Emerging: mentions X-rays and bones without any mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the effect of increasing the frequency of an EM wave while it travels in a vacuum?
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: The wavelength decreases and the energy per photon increases. Distractors: The wavelength increases and the speed increases; The wavelength increases and the energy per photon decreases; The speed decreases and the wavelength stays the same.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the risks and benefits of using gamma radiation in cancer treatment. Refer to the properties of gamma rays in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that gamma rays are highly penetrating and can be focused on a tumour from multiple angles so healthy tissue receives a lower dose; gamma rays damage DNA in cancer cells, killing them; risks include damage to surrounding healthy tissue, increased cancer risk from radiation, and careful dose management is required; concludes with a justified judgement weighing benefit (treating cancer, potentially saving life) against managed risk. Secure: identifies benefits (kills cancer cells, penetrating) and risks (damages healthy tissue) with some detail. Developing: states benefits and risks but without linking properties of gamma to the mechanism. Emerging: vague benefits/risks without scientific detail.

practice_questions.text:
What happens to the temperature of a substance during a change of state, such as melting?
A) It rises steadily
B) It falls steadily
C) It stays constant
D) It rises then falls
practice_questions.marks: C) It stays constant [1 mark — all energy goes into changing potential energy, not kinetic energy, so temperature does not change]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between specific heat capacity and specific latent heat.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C, without a change of state (1). Specific latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg at constant temperature, with no temperature change (1). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Calculate the energy needed to heat 3.0 kg of aluminium from 20 °C to 120 °C. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/(kg °C). Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Correct equation: ΔE = mcΔθ (1). Correct temperature change: Δθ = 120 − 20 = 100 °C (1). Correct substitution: ΔE = 3.0 × 900 × 100 (1). Correct answer with unit: 270 000 J (or 270 kJ) (1). [4 marks — common errors: using 120 instead of 100 for Δθ; missing the unit]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the temperature stays constant during boiling, even though energy is being continuously supplied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: During boiling, energy transferred to the liquid goes into increasing the potential energy of the particles, not their kinetic energy; the particles need energy to overcome the forces of attraction between them and break away from the liquid; because kinetic energy does not increase, the average kinetic energy of the particles (and therefore the temperature) remains constant.
Secure: Energy going into potential energy (breaking bonds) rather than kinetic energy, linked to constant temperature.
Developing: States that energy is used for the change of state but does not mention kinetic/potential energy distinction.
Emerging: States temperature stays constant with no mechanism. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: How much energy is released when 2.0 kg of steam at 100 °C condenses to liquid water at 100 °C? The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2 260 000 J/kg. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Correct equation: E = mL (1). Correct substitution: E = 2.0 × 2 260 000 (1). Correct answer: 4 520 000 J (or 4520 kJ or 4.52 MJ) (1). Correct unit stated (1). Note: energy is released (not absorbed) during condensation — full marks if candidate notes the direction correctly. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A student heats a block of iron using an electrical heater. The joulemeter shows 16 200 J of energy was supplied. The mass of the iron block is 2.0 kg and its temperature rose from 25 °C to 43 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of iron from this data.
practice_questions.marks: Correct equation rearranged: c = ΔE / (m × Δθ) (1). Correct temperature change: Δθ = 43 − 25 = 18 °C (1). Correct substitution: c = 16 200 / (2.0 × 18) = 16 200 / 36 (1). Correct answer with unit: 450 J/(kg °C) (1). [4 marks — common errors: using 43 not 18 for Δθ; missing the unit; rearranging incorrectly]

practice_questions.text: State the name of the blood vessel that carries blood away from the kidney.
practice_questions.marks: Renal vein. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during ultrafiltration in the kidney.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: High blood pressure in the glomerulus forces small molecules (water, glucose, urea, mineral ions) out of the blood and through the capillary walls into the Bowman's capsule to form the filtrate (1); large molecules such as proteins and blood cells are too big to pass through and remain in the blood (1). Emerging: Vague — e.g. 'blood is filtered' without identifying what passes through.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain how ADH brings about a change in urine concentration when a person becomes dehydrated.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: When blood becomes more concentrated (dehydration), osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect this (1); more ADH is released from the pituitary gland (1); ADH makes the kidney tubules more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood, producing a small volume of concentrated urine (1). Secure: Two points correctly linked. Developing: States 'ADH causes concentrated urine' without explaining the mechanism. Emerging: No mechanistic detail.

practice_questions.text: A dialysis patient's blood urea concentration is measured before and after a dialysis session. Before: 28 mmol/L. After: 6 mmol/L. Calculate the percentage decrease in urea concentration. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Decrease = 28 − 6 = 22 mmol/L (1); percentage decrease = (22 ÷ 28) × 100 (1) = 78.57...% (1); rounded to 78.6% (1). Penalise missing % sign or incorrect rounding.

practice_questions.text: Explain why dialysis fluid contains glucose but no urea.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The dialysis fluid contains glucose at the same concentration as normal blood (1); this prevents glucose from diffusing out of the blood across the partially permeable membrane, so the patient does not lose glucose (1); the fluid contains no urea, so urea diffuses from the blood (higher concentration) into the dialysis fluid (lower concentration) down the concentration gradient, removing it from the blood (1). Secure: Two of the three points. Developing: States 'so glucose is not lost' and 'urea moves out' with no reference to concentration gradients. Emerging: One point.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of a kidney transplant compared to long-term dialysis for a patient with kidney failure.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Transplant advantages — kidney functions normally, so the patient no longer needs time-consuming dialysis sessions; quality of life is typically much better; no ongoing cost per session; can eat a more normal diet. Transplant disadvantages — immunosuppressant drugs must be taken for life, increasing infection risk; the operation itself carries surgical risk; suitable donors are scarce. Dialysis advantages — widely available; no surgery required; does not rely on a donor. Dialysis disadvantages — requires sessions several times per week, each lasting several hours; dietary restrictions must be maintained; long-term quality of life is generally lower. A justified conclusion that weighs both sides, noting that a successful transplant is generally preferred but is limited by donor availability and rejection risk. Secure: Four points with some evaluation. Developing: Two advantages and one disadvantage with limited evaluation. Emerging: One point.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes an isotope?
A) An atom of a different element with the same mass number
B) An atom of the same element with the same number of neutrons
C) An atom of the same element with a different number of neutrons
D) An atom of a different element with the same atomic number
practice_questions.marks: C) An atom of the same element with a different number of neutrons [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the charge and approximate relative mass of a neutron.
practice_questions.marks: Charge: 0 (neutral). Relative mass: 1. Both required for the mark. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the results of the alpha scattering experiment led scientists to develop a new model of the atom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description of at least two key observations and the conclusion each supports. E.g. most alpha particles passed straight through (atom is mostly empty space) AND some bounced back at large angles (small, dense, positive nucleus exists).
Secure: Two observations stated with correct conclusions.
Developing: One observation with a correct conclusion.
Emerging: Vague reference to the experiment without linking observations to conclusions.

practice_questions.text: Explain why isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties but different physical properties.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Same chemical properties because isotopes have the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration, so they form the same types of bonds. Different physical properties (e.g. density, mass) because they have different numbers of neutrons and therefore different mass numbers.
Secure: Chemical properties linked to same electrons/electronic configuration; physical differences linked to different mass.
Developing: Identifies same chemical and different physical properties but link to structure is incomplete.
Emerging: States that isotopes differ only in neutron number without explaining the consequences.

practice_questions.text: An atom of phosphorus has atomic number 15 and mass number 31. Calculate the number of neutrons in the nucleus and write the electronic configuration of a neutral phosphorus atom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Neutrons = 31 − 15 = 16 [1]; Electronic configuration 2, 8, 5 [1] with correct method shown [1] and units/notation correct [1].
Secure: Correct number of neutrons and electronic configuration with method shown.
Developing: Correct neutron count OR correct electronic configuration but not both.
Emerging: Substitutes correctly into formula but makes arithmetic error.

practice_questions.text: Describe the development of the atomic model from Dalton to Bohr, explaining what experimental evidence caused each major change. Include at least three scientists in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Chronological account covering at least three scientists (e.g. Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford/Geiger-Marsden, Bohr). Each model change is linked to specific experimental evidence. Language is precise and scientific.
Secure: Three scientists named with their models described; experimental evidence given for at least two model changes.
Developing: Two scientists and their models described; limited reference to experimental evidence.
Emerging: One or two scientists named but models and evidence are vague or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Name one biotic factor that could reduce the size of a rabbit population in a grassland ecosystem.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: increase in predator numbers (e.g. foxes); outbreak of disease; competition from another herbivore species. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Describe how energy is lost between trophic levels in a food chain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Energy is lost through respiration (transferred as heat to the surroundings) (1) and through waste products such as faeces and urine (1). Secure: One point clearly stated. Emerging: Vague — e.g. 'energy is used up' without identifying the mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain why removing a predator from a food web can harm the ecosystem even though predators are not directly providing energy to plants.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Removing the predator causes its prey (herbivore) population to increase, as predation pressure is reduced (1); the expanding herbivore population over-consumes the producer (plant) trophic level, reducing plant biomass (1); this destabilises the ecosystem and may lead to further species declines throughout the food web (1). Secure: Two well-linked points. Developing: States herbivores increase and plants decrease but does not link these steps clearly. Emerging: Restates the question with no mechanistic explanation.

practice_questions.text: In a grassland ecosystem, producers capture 20,000 kJ of energy. Primary consumers obtain 2,400 kJ and secondary consumers obtain 310 kJ. Calculate the percentage efficiency of energy transfer from primary consumers to secondary consumers. Show your working and give your answer to 1 decimal place.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Efficiency = (310 ÷ 2400) × 100 (1 for correct formula applied); = 12.916...% (1 for correct calculation); = 12.9% (1 for correct rounding to 1 d.p.); unit is % — do not penalise if implicit, but award (1) only if answer is clearly a percentage. Secure: Correct method with minor arithmetic error. Note: Do not use 20,000 kJ in the denominator — that is the producers' level, not primary consumers'.

practice_questions.text: Explain how lichen can be used as an indicator of air pollution in an urban area.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Lichens are highly sensitive to sulfur dioxide (air pollution) and are absent or rare in heavily polluted areas (1); if lichen diversity or abundance decreases as you move towards the city centre, this indicates rising air pollution levels (1); different lichen species have different tolerances, so mapping species distribution gives a detailed picture of pollution gradients (1). Secure: Two points. Developing: States 'lichens die in pollution' without explaining the monitoring method. Emerging: One relevant point.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of biodiversity to the stability of an ecosystem. Use examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: High biodiversity means there are multiple species at each trophic level, so if one species declines there are alternatives to fill its role — the food web is more resilient (e.g. a predator can switch prey species). This reduces the risk of cascade effects where the loss of one species destabilises the whole community. Low biodiversity (e.g. a monoculture agricultural field) is fragile — disease or environmental change affecting the one producer species threatens all consumers above it. Biodiversity also maintains ecosystem services (pollination, decomposition, water purification) that underpin human survival. A strong conclusion evaluating how biodiversity acts as an ecological insurance against environmental change. Secure: Four points with examples. Developing: Two points with limited examples or evaluation. Emerging: One point.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a product of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
A) Water
B) Lactic acid
C) Ethanol
D) Glycogen
practice_questions.marks: C) Ethanol [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State where in the cell aerobic respiration takes place.
practice_questions.marks: Mitochondria [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration in animal cells.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for any two of the following:
• Aerobic respiration requires oxygen; anaerobic does not (1)
• Aerobic respiration takes place in mitochondria; anaerobic takes place in the cytoplasm (1)
• Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic produces lactic acid (1)
• Aerobic respiration produces a larger yield of ATP than anaerobic (1)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'oxygen debt' and describe how the body repays it after intense exercise.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• During intense exercise, muscles switch to anaerobic respiration and lactic acid builds up (1)
• Oxygen debt is the extra oxygen required after exercise to break down / oxidise the accumulated lactic acid (1)
• The body repays the debt by continuing to breathe heavily after exercise, supplying oxygen to the liver where lactic acid is converted back to glucose or broken down to carbon dioxide and water (1)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A student sets up an experiment to investigate the rate of fermentation in yeast at different temperatures. At 30°C, the yeast produces 40 cm³ of CO₂ in 5 minutes. At 40°C, it produces 70 cm³ in 5 minutes. Calculate the rate of CO₂ production at each temperature in cm³/min and explain which temperature shows a higher rate of anaerobic respiration.
practice_questions.marks:
Rate at 30°C = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 cm³/min (1)
Rate at 40°C = 70 ÷ 5 = 14 cm³/min (1)
40°C shows a higher rate (1)
Because at higher temperature, yeast enzymes have greater kinetic energy and collide more frequently with substrate, increasing the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions / approaching the optimum temperature (1)
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of respiration in the synthesis of biological molecules. Include reference to carbohydrates, proteins and lipids in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (up to 6 marks):
• Respiration transfers energy from glucose to ATP (1)
• This energy is used to drive the synthesis of biological molecules (1)
• Glucose monomers join together to form carbohydrate polymers: starch (storage in plants) and glycogen (storage in animals, liver and muscles) (1)
• Amino acids are joined in specific sequences (coded for by DNA) to form proteins; the sequence determines the protein's shape and function (1)
• Fatty acids and glycerol combine to form lipids, used for energy storage, cell membranes and thermal insulation (1)
• When energy is needed, these molecules can be broken back down — e.g. glycogen is hydrolysed to glucose which is then respired (1)

StudyVault Mastering: all three molecule classes covered with monomers named and roles linked to function.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the moment produced by a force of 25 N acting at a perpendicular distance of 0.60 m from a pivot.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Moment = force × perpendicular distance; moment = 25 × 0.60 = 15 N m; units stated.
Secure: Correct calculation with unit omitted or one minor error.
Developing: Equation recalled but values inverted or units incorrect.
Emerging: Numbers multiplied but no equation stated and no units.

practice_questions.text: State the principle of moments.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for: for an object in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about a pivot equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same pivot.

practice_questions.text: A beam is balanced on a pivot. A force of 120 N acts 0.50 m to the left of the pivot. Calculate the force needed at 0.30 m to the right of the pivot to keep the beam balanced.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Anticlockwise moment = 120 × 0.50 = 60 N m; applies principle of moments: F × 0.30 = 60; F = 60 ÷ 0.30 = 200 N. Units throughout; equilibrium condition explicitly stated.
Secure: Correct method with one arithmetic error; result follows from working.
Developing: Clockwise moment calculated correctly; rearrangement to find F attempted but incomplete.
Emerging: Identifies principle of moments but cannot set up the equation.

practice_questions.text: A driving gear has 20 teeth and a driven gear has 80 teeth. The driving gear rotates at 300 rpm. Calculate the rotation speed of the driven gear and state whether its turning force is greater or smaller than the driving gear.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gear ratio = 80 ÷ 20 = 4; driven gear speed = 300 ÷ 4 = 75 rpm; states that the driven gear has a greater turning force (moment) because the ratio >1.
Secure: Speed calculated correctly; turning force comparison correct but not explained.
Developing: Gear ratio correct; speed calculation attempted but error.
Emerging: Identifies that the larger gear rotates more slowly but cannot calculate the speed.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lever can be used to lift a heavy object with a small force, using the principle of moments in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A lever pivots about a fulcrum; applying a small force at a large perpendicular distance from the pivot creates a large moment (moment = F × d); by the principle of moments, this large moment can balance and lift a heavy load positioned close to the pivot (which has a smaller moment arm), so the effort force needed is much less than the load.
Secure: Identifies force multiplication; links to moment equation and principle of moments.
Developing: States levers multiply force with reference to pivot; does not link to moments equation.
Emerging: States levers make it easier to lift objects with no scientific explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe the practical investigation that could be carried out to verify the principle of moments using a metre ruler, pivot and hanging masses.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes balancing a metre ruler on a pivot at the centre; hanging known masses at measured distances on both sides; measuring the perpendicular distance from each mass to the pivot; calculating clockwise and anticlockwise moments (moment = weight × distance, where weight = mass × g); showing that clockwise moments total equals anticlockwise moments total when balanced; repeating with different masses/distances to confirm the principle. Identifies control variables (pivot position fixed); describes how to reduce uncertainty (use several masses, precise measurement of distances).
Secure: Most steps correct; moment calculation included; conclusion linked to principle of moments.
Developing: Describes balancing masses on a ruler; mentions moments but calculation or conclusion incomplete.
Emerging: General description of a balance activity with limited scientific content.

practice_questions.text: State what happens to the speed of a light ray when it passes from air into glass.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: the speed decreases (light slows down in glass compared to air).

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the focal point of a converging lens.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: the point on the principal axis where parallel rays of light converge after passing through the lens. 1 mark: located on the far side of the lens from the incoming light, at a distance equal to the focal length.

practice_questions.text: A converging lens has a focal length of 0.2 m. An object is placed 0.5 m from the lens. Without drawing a diagram, state whether the image formed is real or virtual, and state whether it is upright or inverted.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: real image (object is beyond the focal point). 1 mark: inverted (real images from a single converging lens are always inverted).

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the idea of refraction, why a glass prism splits white light into a range of colours.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that white light is made up of different wavelengths (colours); different wavelengths travel at different speeds in glass so they refract by different amounts; violet light refracts more than red light, causing the colours to spread out and form a spectrum. Secure: states different colours refract by different amounts in glass, producing a spectrum. Developing: states the prism separates colours but does not explain why different colours refract differently. Emerging: mentions refraction without linking it to wavelength or colour.

practice_questions.text: An object is placed between the focal point and the lens of a converging lens. Which of the following best describes the image formed?
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: Virtual, upright and magnified. Distractors: Real, inverted and magnified; Real, inverted and diminished; Virtual, inverted and diminished.

practice_questions.text: Draw and describe the ray diagram for a converging lens forming a real image of an object placed beyond twice the focal length. Include the three principal rays, label the image, and describe its characteristics.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: draws all three principal rays correctly (parallel ray through far focal point; central ray straight; near-focal-point ray emerging parallel); rays converge to form image beyond 2f on the far side; image correctly labelled as real, inverted, diminished; diagram is neat with principal axis, lens, both focal points and object labelled. Secure: draws two or three rays with minor errors; image correctly placed with two characteristics stated. Developing: one ray correct; image placed approximately correctly; at least one characteristic stated. Emerging: lens and focal points drawn but ray paths largely incorrect.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a property of all Group 1 elements?
A) They are non-metals
B) They have two electrons in their outer shell
C) They react with water to produce hydrogen gas
D) Their reactivity decreases going down the group
practice_questions.marks: C) They react with water to produce hydrogen gas [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the flame test colour for sodium and for potassium.
practice_questions.marks: Sodium: yellow (or orange-yellow). Potassium: lilac (or violet). Both required for the mark. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what you would observe when chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes visible colour change (solution turns orange or brown) AND identifies that bromine has been displaced/formed.
Secure: Identifies colour change and states bromine is produced.
Developing: States a colour change but does not explain which substance caused it.
Emerging: States “a reaction occurs” without describing what is observed.

practice_questions.text: Explain why potassium is more reactive with water than lithium.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Potassium’s outer electron is in a higher energy level, further from the nucleus. There is more electron shielding from inner shells. The electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker. Therefore the outer electron is lost more easily, making potassium more reactive.
Secure: Outer electron further from nucleus, less strongly held, more easily lost.
Developing: States outer electron is further away but does not link to ease of losing it.
Emerging: Just states “potassium is lower in the group” without an explanation.

practice_questions.text: Bromine has atomic number 35 and exists as Br2 molecules. Predict whether bromine will react with potassium iodide solution. Write a balanced symbol equation for any reaction that occurs and explain your reasoning.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly predicts that bromine will react (more reactive than iodine) [1]. Balanced equation: Br2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KBr(aq) + I2(aq) [1]. Explains bromine is more reactive because its outer shell is closer to the nucleus, making it easier to gain an electron [1]. States this is a displacement reaction [1].
Secure: Correct prediction with balanced equation and a linked explanation.
Developing: Correct prediction and equation but explanation is incomplete.
Emerging: Correct prediction but equation unbalanced and little explanation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how well Mendeleev’s early periodic table predicted the existence and properties of undiscovered elements. Refer to specific examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Discusses Mendeleev leaving gaps; explains he predicted density, melting point and compounds for missing elements; gives example(s) such as gallium or germanium; evaluates that subsequent discoveries confirmed his predictions, validating the table as a predictive tool not just a classification. Considers limitations (e.g. occasional need to swap elements, later refined by atomic number).
Secure: Explains gaps and predictions, names at least one element, links discovery to validation.
Developing: Explains gaps but examples are vague; limited evaluation.
Emerging: Describes Mendeleev’s table in general terms without specifics.

practice_questions.text:
Which flame test colour is produced by sodium ions?
A) Crimson
B) Lilac
C) Yellow
D) Green
practice_questions.marks: C) Yellow [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the test used to identify carbon dioxide gas and the observation that confirms its presence.
practice_questions.marks: Bubble through limewater; it turns milky / cloudy (white precipitate forms). [1 mark — both test and observation required]

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would test an unknown solution to determine whether it contains iron(II) or iron(III) ions.
practice_questions.marks: Add sodium hydroxide solution to the unknown solution [1 mark]; iron(II) ions give a green precipitate; iron(III) ions give a brown precipitate [1 mark — must distinguish between the two colours].

practice_questions.text: A student adds silver nitrate solution to two unknown solutions and observes a cream precipitate in one and a yellow precipitate in the other. Explain what ions are present in each solution and why the student must acidify the solutions before adding silver nitrate.
practice_questions.marks: Cream precipitate = bromide ions (Br⁻) [1 mark]; yellow precipitate = iodide ions (I⁻) [1 mark]; acidifying (with dilute nitric acid) removes carbonate ions or other ions that would form precipitates with silver nitrate and give misleading results [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
An unknown ionic compound is dissolved in water. A flame test produces an orange-red colour. Adding sodium hydroxide solution produces a white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess NaOH.

(a) Identify the metal ion present. [1 mark]
(b) Explain how you would determine whether a sulfate ion is present in the solution. [3 marks]
practice_questions.marks: (a) Calcium (Ca²⁺) — orange-red flame, white precipitate with NaOH that does not dissolve [1 mark]; (b) Add dilute hydrochloric acid to remove any carbonate ions that might interfere [1 mark]; add barium chloride solution [1 mark]; a white precipitate of barium sulfate (BaSO₄) confirms sulfate ions are present [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Describe how instrumental methods of analysis, such as flame emission spectroscopy, differ from traditional chemical tests such as the flame test. Include the advantages of instrumental methods and explain when a traditional flame test might give a misleading result.

Include detail on how flame emission spectroscopy works.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear explanation that flame emission spectroscopy separates light from the flame into a spectrum of characteristic wavelength lines unique to each element; can identify mixtures because each element contributes its own spectral lines (unlike a single-colour flame test which can be masked by sodium yellow); gives quantitative information from line intensity; much higher sensitivity for detecting trace amounts. Traditional flame test limitations clearly stated: cannot distinguish mixtures, qualitative only, relies on human colour perception. Specific example of sodium masking potassium in a flame test.
Secure: Two or more advantages of instrumental methods correctly stated; limitation of flame test noted; how emission spectroscopy produces a spectrum described.
Developing: One advantage identified; some mention of spectrum or sensitivity; flame test limitation noted.
Emerging: Basic comparison made; limited detail on how either method works.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a vector quantity?
A) Speed
B) Distance
C) Mass
D) Velocity
practice_questions.marks:
D) Velocity [1 mark]
Velocity has both magnitude and direction, making it a vector. Speed, distance and mass are all scalars.

practice_questions.text: State the equation used to calculate acceleration from initial velocity, final velocity, and time.
practice_questions.marks:
a = (v − u) ÷ t [1 mark]
Where a = acceleration (m/s²), v = final velocity (m/s), u = initial velocity (m/s), t = time (s).

practice_questions.text: A car travels at a constant speed of 18 m/s and then brakes, coming to rest in 9 seconds. Calculate the deceleration of the car. Give your answer in m/s².
practice_questions.marks:
Identify values: u = 18 m/s, v = 0 m/s, t = 9 s [1 mark]
Apply equation: a = (v − u) ÷ t [1 mark]
a = (0 − 18) ÷ 9 = −2 m/s² [1 mark]
Deceleration = 2 m/s² (accept −2 m/s²; award final mark for correct unit) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A distance-time graph shows a straight line with a positive gradient, followed by a horizontal section, and then a steeper straight line with a positive gradient.
Describe the motion of the object during each section.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three sections described accurately — constant speed (gradient = speed), stationary (horizontal = zero speed), then faster constant speed (steeper gradient = greater speed). [2 marks]
Secure: Two sections described correctly. [2 marks]
Developing: One section described correctly. [1 mark]
Emerging: Vague reference to motion with no use of gradient. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain what happens to the acceleration and velocity of a skydiver from the moment they jump to when they reach terminal velocity. Refer to the forces acting on the skydiver.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies weight > air resistance initially → resultant force downwards → acceleration. As speed increases, air resistance increases. When air resistance = weight, resultant force = zero, acceleration = zero, terminal velocity reached. Correct direction of all forces stated. [3 marks]
Secure: States weight and air resistance, mentions resultant force = zero at terminal velocity, some description of changing acceleration. [2 marks]
Developing: Mentions two forces but does not explain how they change or link to resultant force. [1 mark]
Emerging: Vague — 'forces balance' without explanation. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text:
(Higher tier) A student plots a velocity-time graph for a ball rolling down a slope and then across a flat surface. The ball reaches the flat surface after 4 seconds with a velocity of 8 m/s, and its velocity stays constant for a further 6 seconds.
Calculate the total distance travelled by the ball in this 10-second journey. You must show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Distance on slope (0–4 s): area of triangle = ½ × 4 × 8 = 16 m [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for value]
Distance on flat (4–10 s): area of rectangle = 6 × 8 = 48 m [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for value]
Total distance = 16 + 48 = 64 m [1 mark]
Unit stated (m) [1 mark]

Mastering: Correct method and answer with units and clear working.
Secure: Correct method for both sections, minor arithmetic error.
Developing: Correct method for one section only.
Emerging: Attempts to use distance = speed × time but does not split into sections.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following describes Newton's First Law of motion?
A) Force equals mass times acceleration
B) Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
C) An object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force
D) The rate of change of momentum equals the resultant force
practice_questions.marks: C) An object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the equation that links weight, mass and gravitational field strength.
practice_questions.marks:
W = m × g [1 mark]
Where W = weight (N), m = mass (kg), g = gravitational field strength (N/kg).

practice_questions.text:
A shopping trolley of mass 25 kg experiences a pushing force of 80 N from a shopper and a friction force of 30 N opposing its motion.
Calculate the acceleration of the trolley.
practice_questions.marks:
Resultant force = 80 − 30 = 50 N [1 mark]
Apply F = ma: a = F ÷ m [1 mark]
a = 50 ÷ 25 = 2 m/s² [1 mark]
Unit: m/s² [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two factors that increase the thinking distance of a driver, and two factors that increase the braking distance of a vehicle.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for any two correct thinking distance factors: tiredness / alcohol / drugs / distraction (e.g. mobile phone) / higher speed. [1 mark]
One mark for any two correct braking distance factors: higher speed / wet or icy roads / worn tyres / faulty brakes / heavier vehicle. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A book rests on a table. Identify the Newton's Third Law pair to the weight of the book. Explain what makes these two forces a Third Law pair.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly identifies the reaction force — the gravitational pull of the book on the Earth (upward). States it is equal in size, opposite in direction, the same type of force (gravitational), and acts on the Earth (a different object). Distinguishes this from the normal contact force, which acts on the same object (the book) and is a different type of force. [3 marks]
Secure: Identifies reaction force and gives two of the four criteria. [2 marks]
Developing: Identifies 'the table pushing up' — this is the normal contact force, not the Third Law pair; gains no marks for identification but may gain 1 mark for criteria. [1 mark]
Emerging: Vague — 'the table pushes the book up' with no discussion of pairs. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'A heavier vehicle always has a longer stopping distance than a lighter vehicle travelling at the same speed.' Evaluate this statement, referring to both thinking distance and braking distance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Considers thinking distance (same for both vehicles at the same speed, as thinking distance depends on reaction time and speed, not mass). Evaluates braking distance (heavier vehicle stores more kinetic energy so needs greater braking force or longer distance to stop). Acknowledges that braking force also depends on road conditions and tyre quality — a heavier vehicle with better brakes or tyres may not necessarily stop in a longer distance. Reaches a justified conclusion with evidence from physics. [5–6 marks]
Secure: Correctly addresses braking distance, less detail on thinking distance, some reasoning. [3–4 marks]
Developing: States heavier = longer stopping distance without physics reasoning. [1–2 marks]
Emerging: Minimal physics content. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a raw material for photosynthesis?
A) Glucose
B) Oxygen
C) Carbon dioxide
D) ATP
practice_questions.marks: C) Carbon dioxide [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two uses of glucose produced by photosynthesis in a plant.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the following (1 mark for any two correct):
• Respiration (to release energy)
• Converted to starch for storage
• Converted to cellulose for cell walls
• Combined with mineral ions to make amino acids / proteins
• Converted to lipids for storage in seeds
[1 mark for two correct answers]

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would use Elodea pondweed to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for any two of the following:
• Place Elodea underwater in a beaker and position a lamp at a measured distance (1)
• Count the number of oxygen bubbles produced per minute (or measure volume of gas collected) at different distances (1)
• Repeat measurements to calculate a mean and improve reliability (1)
• Control variables such as temperature and CO₂ concentration (e.g. add sodium hydrogencarbonate to water) (1)
[2 marks — any two valid points]

practice_questions.text: Explain why increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis up to a point, but then has no further effect.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Increasing CO₂ provides more raw material for the carbon fixation stage of photosynthesis (1)
• This allows more glucose to be produced per unit time, so the rate increases (1)
• The rate levels off when another factor — light intensity or temperature — becomes limiting / when the enzymes are working at maximum rate (1)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) A lamp is placed 10 cm from a piece of Elodea. The rate of photosynthesis is measured as 80 bubbles per minute. The lamp is moved to 40 cm away. Use the inverse square law to calculate the expected rate of photosynthesis at 40 cm. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Light intensity is proportional to 1/d² (1)
At 10 cm: relative intensity = 1/10² = 1/100 = 0.01
At 40 cm: relative intensity = 1/40² = 1/1600 = 0.000625 (1)
Ratio: 0.000625 ÷ 0.01 = 1/16 (distance increased by factor 4, so intensity drops by factor 16) (1)
Expected rate = 80 ÷ 16 = 5 bubbles per minute (1)
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a farmer could use knowledge of limiting factors to increase the yield of tomatoes grown in a greenhouse.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (up to 6 marks):
• Light intensity: artificial lighting extends the growing day and increases light intensity, providing more energy for photosynthesis (1)
• Carbon dioxide: burning gas heaters or pumping in CO₂ increases CO₂ concentration, providing more raw material for photosynthesis (1)
• Temperature: heaters maintain an optimal temperature for photosynthesis enzymes to work at their fastest without denaturing (1)
• All three factors must be at sufficient levels simultaneously — increasing one factor has no effect if another is already limiting (1)
• The farmer must balance the cost of providing these conditions against the extra income from improved yield (1)
• Tomatoes produced using optimal conditions grow faster, giving more harvests per year (1)

StudyVault Mastering: all three factors discussed with cost-benefit consideration and the limiting factor concept applied to the practical context.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following explains why increasing temperature increases the rate of reaction?
A) Particles become smaller so they can collide more easily
B) Particles have more energy, so more collisions have sufficient energy to react
C) The activation energy decreases as temperature increases
D) Particles dissolve more readily at higher temperatures
practice_questions.marks: B) Particles have more energy, so more collisions have sufficient energy to react [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which you could increase the rate of a reaction between marble chips (calcium carbonate) and hydrochloric acid.
practice_questions.marks: Any two of: increase temperature; increase concentration of acid; crush/grind the marble chips into a powder (increase surface area); add a catalyst. [1 mark for any two correct]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a gas syringe can be used to measure the rate of the reaction between magnesium ribbon and dilute hydrochloric acid.
practice_questions.marks: Collect hydrogen gas produced in a gas syringe connected to the reaction flask [1 mark]; record the volume of gas at regular time intervals (e.g. every 30 seconds) and plot volume against time [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain how increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid increases the rate of its reaction with magnesium ribbon, using ideas from collision theory.
practice_questions.marks: Increasing concentration means there are more acid particles (H⁺ ions) in the same volume [1 mark]; the frequency of collisions between H⁺ ions and magnesium particles increases [1 mark]; so more successful collisions occur per unit time and the rate increases [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
A student investigates how the surface area of marble chips affects the rate of reaction with dilute hydrochloric acid. She uses the same mass of marble in each experiment but varies the size of the chips.

(a) Identify the independent variable, dependent variable, and one control variable in this investigation. [3 marks]
(b) The student collects the gas using a gas syringe and records the volume every 30 seconds. Sketch the shape of the graph she would expect if small chips react faster than large chips, but the same total volume of gas is produced in both experiments. [1 mark]
