practice_questions.marks: (a) Independent: size/surface area of marble chips [1 mark]; dependent: volume of gas produced / rate of reaction [1 mark]; control: mass of marble, volume/concentration of acid, temperature [1 mark — any one]; (b) Two curves levelling off at the same point: the small chips curve is steeper initially (faster rate) but both curves level off at the same final volume of gas [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction. In your answer, include:
• what a catalyst does to the activation energy
• how this is shown on a reaction profile
• what happens to the catalyst at the end of the reaction
• why different reactions require different catalysts.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy [1 mark]; on the reaction profile this is shown as a lower peak / smaller hump, while reactant and product energy levels are unchanged [1 mark]; a greater proportion of collisions now have sufficient energy to react, increasing the rate [1 mark]; catalyst is not used up / not permanently changed at the end [1 mark]; catalysts are specific because the alternative pathway depends on the interaction between the catalyst's active site/surface and particular reactant molecules [1 mark]; overall energy change of the reaction is not affected by the catalyst [1 mark].
Secure: Most of the above correctly stated; reaction profile correctly described; catalyst specificity noted.
Developing: Activation energy lowered and catalyst not used up both stated; profile or specificity partially addressed.
Emerging: Basic statement that catalyst speeds up reactions; limited mechanistic explanation.

practice_questions.text:
A student measures the melting point of a sample of aspirin and finds it melts over the range 128–133°C. The expected melting point of pure aspirin is 135°C. What conclusion can be drawn?
A) The sample is pure aspirin
B) The sample is impure and contains at least one other substance
C) The sample is pure but has been stored incorrectly
D) The melting point range proves the substance is not aspirin
practice_questions.marks: B) The sample is impure and contains at least one other substance [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two separation techniques that could be used to obtain pure solid copper sulfate crystals from a solution of copper sulfate in water.
practice_questions.marks: Evaporation/heating to reduce volume, then crystallisation (slow cooling). Both steps required for the mark, or crystallisation alone accepted. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would use paper chromatography to find out whether a food colouring is a mixture of dyes or a single pure dye.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes drawing a pencil baseline, placing a spot of food colouring on the line, placing paper in solvent (below baseline), allowing solvent to rise, then interpreting the result: single spot = pure dye, multiple spots = mixture.
Secure: Covers method and interpretation clearly.
Developing: Describes the method but does not explain how to interpret the results.
Emerging: Vague description of “put it in solvent and see what happens.”

practice_questions.text: Explain why simple distillation is used to obtain pure water from sea water, and why fractional distillation would not be needed for this process.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sea water is a solution of salts dissolved in water. Simple distillation heats the sea water, the water evaporates and is condensed, leaving the dissolved salts behind. Fractional distillation is not needed because there is only one liquid (water) to separate from a non-volatile dissolved solid; fractional distillation is required when separating two or more liquids with different boiling points.
Secure: Correct explanation of simple distillation with reason why fractional distillation is unnecessary.
Developing: Explains simple distillation correctly but does not address why fractional distillation is unnecessary.
Emerging: States that water evaporates without explaining the technique.

practice_questions.text: In a chromatography experiment, a yellow food dye produces a spot that moves 5.4 cm. The solvent front moves 9.0 cm. A reference sample of tartrazine produces a spot that moves 5.4 cm under identical conditions. Calculate the Rf value of the food dye and state whether the food dye could be tartrazine.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Rf = 5.4 ÷ 9.0 = 0.60 [1]. Units: Rf has no units [1]. Rf of dye matches Rf of tartrazine (0.60) so the dye could be tartrazine [1]. Acknowledges this is not conclusive proof (would need to test in multiple solvents) [1].
Secure: Correct Rf calculated, correctly concluded that the dye could be tartrazine.
Developing: Correct calculation but conclusion not clearly stated.
Emerging: Substitutes values but makes arithmetic or formula error.

practice_questions.text: Paints are described as formulations. Explain what this means, and discuss how knowing that a mixture is a formulation rather than a pure substance affects how it would be tested for purity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines formulation as a mixture with each component in a precise measured amount to give specific properties. Names components of paint (e.g. pigment, binder, solvent). Explains that a formulation is not pure in the chemical sense, so it would melt over a range of temperatures, not at a single sharp point. A pure substance would melt sharply. Discusses that chromatography could separate the dye components of the paint. Evaluates that purity testing applies to individual components, not the formulation as a whole.
Secure: Defines formulation with examples, explains effect on melting point, links to testing method.
Developing: Defines formulation and states melting occurs over a range, but limited evaluation.
Emerging: Describes formulations vaguely without linking to purity testing.

practice_questions.text: State how many chromosomes are found in a human gamete.
practice_questions.marks: 23 chromosomes. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which meiosis produces genetically different cells.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Chromosomes are shuffled during the first division (independent assortment) so different combinations of chromosomes enter each new cell (1); crossing over (exchange of sections between homologous chromosomes) produces new combinations of alleles within each chromosome (1). Secure: Two valid points, may use simpler language. Developing: States 'the cells are all different' without explaining the mechanism. Emerging: One point.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain how the sequence of bases in a gene determines the characteristics of an organism.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The base sequence of a gene determines the sequence of amino acids assembled during protein synthesis (1); amino acid sequence determines the shape and therefore the function of the protein produced (1); proteins include enzymes, hormones and structural components that ultimately control the characteristics (phenotype) of the organism (1). Secure: Two points clearly linked. Developing: States 'genes code for proteins which control characteristics' without explaining the mechanism. Emerging: Vague or circular definition.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) A section of DNA template strand has the base sequence: T-A-C-G-G-A. Write the complementary mRNA sequence that would be produced during transcription. Remember that uracil (U) replaces thymine in RNA.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A-U-G-C-C-U (1 mark per correct pair, up to 3 marks); all six bases correctly identified = 3 marks; correct use of U instead of T in mRNA (1 additional mark for no T appearing in the mRNA sequence). Total: 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why sexual reproduction produces offspring with greater variation than asexual reproduction.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: In sexual reproduction, meiosis shuffles chromosomes during gamete formation, producing gametes with unique combinations of alleles (1); fertilisation combines gametes from two parents, further increasing genetic diversity (1); asexual reproduction uses mitosis, producing offspring with identical genetic material to the parent (clones), so no new variation is generated (1). Secure: Two points. Developing: States 'sexual reproduction mixes genes from two parents' without explaining meiosis or fertilisation. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Describe the process of translation and explain how it produces a functional protein from the mRNA code.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The mRNA strand produced during transcription moves from the nucleus to the cytoplasm and attaches to a ribosome. The ribosome reads the mRNA code in triplets (codons). Each codon corresponds to a specific amino acid. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry specific amino acids; the anticodon on each tRNA is complementary to the mRNA codon, so the correct amino acid is brought to the ribosome. The ribosome catalyses the formation of peptide bonds between successive amino acids, building a growing polypeptide chain. When a stop codon is reached, the chain is released and folds into a specific three-dimensional shape determined by its amino acid sequence. This shape determines the protein's function (e.g. active site of an enzyme). A well-structured answer that connects each step clearly. Secure: Four steps described. Developing: Mentions ribosomes and amino acids but misses tRNA or codon/anticodon. Emerging: One or two steps with no mechanism.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly states the equation for pressure?
A) p = F × A
B) p = A / F
C) p = F / A
D) p = F × A²
practice_questions.marks: C) p = F / A [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the SI unit of pressure and give its equivalent in base SI units.
practice_questions.marks: Pascal (Pa); equivalent to N/m² (newton per square metre). [1 mark — accept either]

practice_questions.text: Describe how pressure in a liquid changes with depth, and explain why this change occurs.
practice_questions.marks: Pressure increases with depth (1). This is because there is a greater weight of liquid above acting on a given area / a greater column of liquid above pressing down (1). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a steel ship floats even though steel is denser than water.
practice_questions.marks: The hollow hull of the ship displaces a large volume of water (1). The weight of water displaced equals the total weight of the ship (1). The upthrust produced equals the ship’s weight, so the ship floats / upthrust = weight (1). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A submarine is 80 m below the surface of seawater. The density of seawater is 1025 kg/m³ and g = 10 N/kg.
(a) Calculate the pressure due to the seawater column at this depth.
(b) The submarine’s hull has a surface area of 420 m² on its upper face at this depth. Calculate the force exerted by the water on this surface.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) p = hρg = 80 × 1025 × 10 = 820 000 Pa (2 marks: 1 for correct substitution, 1 for correct answer with units)
(b) F = p × A = 820 000 × 420 = 344 400 000 N = 3.44 × 10⁸ N (2 marks: 1 for correct rearrangement and substitution, 1 for correct answer with units) [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: A student claims: ‘When you drink through a straw, suction pulls the liquid up.’ Evaluate this claim, referring to the concept of atmospheric pressure and the pressure difference created inside the straw.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Correctly identifies that ‘suction’ is a misleading description. Explains that breathing in reduces the air pressure inside the straw. States that atmospheric pressure acting on the liquid surface outside the straw is now greater than the pressure inside. Explains that this pressure difference produces a net upward force on the liquid, pushing it up the straw. Refers to the liquid being pushed rather than pulled. May note that atmospheric pressure at sea level is approximately 101 000 Pa and that the pressure difference drives the liquid upwards.
Secure (3–4 marks): Correctly identifies the role of pressure difference. States that pressure inside the straw is reduced, and atmospheric pressure outside is greater. Explains liquid is pushed up, not pulled, but lacks full mechanistic explanation.
Developing (1–2 marks): Recognises that pressure is involved but explanation is incomplete or partially incorrect. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: State the change in mass number and atomic number when a nucleus undergoes beta decay.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: mass number unchanged. 1 mark: atomic number increases by 1.

practice_questions.text:
Complete the nuclear equation for the alpha decay of radium-226 (atomic number 88):
²²⁶₈₈Ra → ? + ⁴₂He
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct mass number 222. 1 mark: correct atomic number 86 (radon). Full answer: ²²²₈₆Rn.

practice_questions.text: A radioactive source has an initial count rate of 1200 counts per minute and a half-life of 8 hours. Calculate the count rate after 24 hours.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: identifies number of half-lives = 24 ÷ 8 = 3. 1 mark: shows repeated halving: 1200 → 600 → 300 → 150. 1 mark: correct answer 150. 1 mark: correct unit (counts per minute).

practice_questions.text: Explain why contamination by an alpha-emitting source is considered particularly hazardous, even though alpha particles are stopped by skin.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that if an alpha source enters the body (inhaled or ingested), the alpha particles are in direct contact with internal tissues; alpha is the most ionising type of radiation so causes maximum damage to cells and DNA at close range; continuous exposure cannot be reduced simply by distance since the source is inside the body. Secure: states alpha causes most ionisation close up, and contamination means the source stays inside the body. Developing: states alpha is dangerous when inside the body without explaining why ionisation causes more damage internally. Emerging: mentions contamination and alpha without distinguishing internal vs external exposure.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following correctly states the penetrating power of the three types of ionising radiation in order from least to most penetrating?
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: Alpha, beta, gamma. Distractors: Gamma, beta, alpha; Beta, alpha, gamma; Alpha, gamma, beta.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of carbon-14 dating as a method of determining the age of ancient organic materials. Include a discussion of its strengths and limitations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that carbon-14 is taken in by living organisms; after death, the proportion of carbon-14 decreases as it decays; by measuring the remaining count rate and using the known half-life of carbon-14, the age can be calculated; strengths include accuracy for samples up to several tens of thousands of years; limitations include that it cannot be used for materials older than this range (activity too low to measure reliably), requires knowledge of the original carbon-14 ratio, and cannot be used for non-organic materials. Secure: explains mechanism and gives one strength and one limitation. Developing: describes basic principle but limitations are vague. Emerging: mentions carbon-14 and age without mechanism.

before.exam_tip_html: Nuclear equation questions require all mass numbers and atomic numbers to balance — check both sides before moving on. For half-life calculations, work methodically: find how many half-lives fit into the total time, then halve the activity that many times. For extended-response questions on the risks of radiation, use the terms contamination and irradiation precisely — examiners reward clear distinction between the two. Remember: alpha is the most ionising but least penetrating; gamma is the least ionising but most penetrating.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the state of dynamic equilibrium?
A) The forward and reverse reactions have stopped
B) The concentrations of reactants and products are equal
C) The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction
D) Only the forward reaction is occurring
practice_questions.marks: C) The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) State the three conditions used in the Haber process.
practice_questions.marks: Approximately 450°C; approximately 200 atm (high pressure); iron catalyst. [1 mark — all three required]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Describe what happens to a system at equilibrium when a product is removed from the reaction mixture.
practice_questions.marks: Removing a product reduces its concentration [1 mark]; the equilibrium shifts in the forward direction (towards products) to replace the product that has been removed [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
(Higher tier) The Haber process reaction is: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) (forward reaction exothermic).

Explain why a low temperature increases the yield of ammonia but is not used industrially.
practice_questions.marks: A low temperature favours the exothermic direction (forward reaction) because Le Chatelier's principle states the equilibrium shifts to release heat and oppose the cooling [1 mark]; this increases the proportion of ammonia at equilibrium (greater yield) [1 mark]; however, a very low temperature slows the rate of reaction so dramatically that the time taken to reach equilibrium becomes commercially unacceptable [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
(Higher tier) The reaction between sulfur dioxide and oxygen is: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)

The forward reaction is exothermic. Predict and explain the effect of each of the following changes on the equilibrium position:
(a) Increasing pressure [2 marks]
(b) Increasing temperature [2 marks]
practice_questions.marks: (a) Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas [1 mark]; the products side has 2 moles of gas vs 3 moles on the reactants side, so equilibrium shifts to the right / more SO₃ is produced [1 mark]; (b) Increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction (reverse reaction) to absorb the extra heat [1 mark]; equilibrium shifts to the left / yield of SO₃ decreases [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
(Higher tier) Explain why the industrial conditions for the Haber process (approximately 450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst) represent a compromise, rather than the conditions that would give the maximum theoretical yield of ammonia.

In your answer, consider the effects of temperature, pressure and the catalyst separately.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Temperature — lowering temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction and gives a higher equilibrium yield of NH₃, but rate becomes too slow at very low temperatures; 450°C is a compromise giving acceptable rate and yield; increasing temperature increases rate but reduces yield. Pressure — higher pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas (products: 2 mol vs reactants: 4 mol) so gives higher yield and rate, but very high pressures are extremely expensive to achieve and maintain and present safety hazards; 200 atm is a compromise. Catalyst — the iron catalyst increases the rate at which equilibrium is reached (both forward and reverse equally) without affecting the equilibrium position or yield; it is used to compensate for the rate reduction caused by the moderate temperature. Unreacted gases recycled to improve overall efficiency.
Secure: All three factors addressed correctly; compromise nature of conditions stated for at least two; catalyst correctly identified as not affecting yield.
Developing: Temperature and pressure discussed; catalyst mentioned; compromise language used for one factor.
Emerging: One or two conditions named; limited explanation of compromise.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes a heterozygous genotype for a gene with alleles A and a?
A) AA
B) Aa
C) aa
D) AB
practice_questions.marks: B) Aa [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term phenotype.
practice_questions.marks:
The observable characteristics of an organism [1 mark]
Accept: the physical appearance of an organism produced by its genotype (and environment)

practice_questions.text:
Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). Two carrier parents (Ff) have a child.
Describe the possible genotypes of the child and state the probability of the child having cystic fibrosis.
practice_questions.marks:
Possible genotypes: FF, Ff, ff [1 mark for identifying all three]
Probability of cystic fibrosis (ff): 25% (or 1 in 4 / 1:4) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Huntington's disease is caused by a dominant allele (H). A parent with genotype Hh has children with an unaffected partner (hh).
Explain why 50% of their children are expected to develop Huntington's disease. Include a genetic diagram in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Parental genotypes: Hh × hh [1 mark]
Gametes shown: H and h from affected parent; h and h from unaffected parent [1 mark]
Offspring: Hh (affected) and hh (unaffected) in 1:1 ratio, so 50% probability of Hh offspring developing the condition; stated because the H allele is dominant so one copy causes disease [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A student has data from crossing two heterozygous plants (Tt × Tt), where T (tall) is dominant over t (dwarf).
Calculate the expected percentage of tall plants in the offspring.
practice_questions.marks:
Parental genotypes: Tt × Tt [1 mark]
Gametes: T and t from each parent [1 mark]
Punnett square completed correctly: TT, Tt, Tt, tt [1 mark]
Tall offspring (TT + Tt) = 3 out of 4 = 75% [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of embryo screening to test for inherited genetic disorders such as cystic fibrosis before implantation during IVF.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation with developed points for and against, clear explanation of how the technique works, and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Arguments on both sides with some development; may lack full explanation of the technique or conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points on one or both sides with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement with little or no evaluation.

Points may include:
For: prevents suffering of children born with serious conditions; allows families at risk to have unaffected biological children; reduces pressure on NHS caring for affected individuals.
Against: raises concerns about selecting embryo characteristics beyond medical need; some argue unused embryos are destroyed, raising ethical objections; risk of social pressure on parents to select; may lead to reduced acceptance of people with disabilities.
Conclusion should weigh severity of condition against ethical concerns.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following describes elastic deformation?
A) The object is permanently changed in shape
B) The object returns to its original shape when the force is removed
C) The object stretches beyond its elastic limit
D) The object compresses without any force applied
practice_questions.marks: B) The object returns to its original shape when the force is removed [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the equation that links moment, force and distance.
practice_questions.marks:
Moment = force × perpendicular distance from pivot [1 mark]
(Accept M = Fd where d is perpendicular distance)

practice_questions.text:
A spring has a natural length of 12.0 cm. When a force of 6.0 N is applied, it stretches to 18.0 cm.
Calculate the spring constant of the spring. Give your answer in N/m.
practice_questions.marks:
Extension = 18.0 − 12.0 = 6.0 cm = 0.06 m [1 mark]
Apply F = ke: k = F ÷ e [1 mark]
k = 6.0 ÷ 0.06 = 100 N/m [1 mark]
Unit: N/m [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would use a spring, masses and a ruler to investigate Hooke's Law in the school laboratory. Include how you would ensure accuracy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes adding masses one at a time, measuring extension each time (not total length), plotting force vs extension, identifying the straight-line region. Mentions parallax-free reading at eye level or repeated readings for accuracy. [2 marks]
Secure: Basic method described but accuracy improvement missing. [1 mark]
Developing: Vague — 'add weights and measure the spring'. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A lever is used to lift a rock. The rock (load) weighs 900 N and is placed 0.4 m from the pivot. An effort force is applied 1.8 m from the pivot on the other side.
Calculate the effort force needed to balance the rock. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Anticlockwise moment (load) = 900 × 0.4 = 360 N m [1 mark]
For equilibrium: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment [1 mark]
Effort × 1.8 = 360 [1 mark]
Effort = 360 ÷ 1.8 = 200 N [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain how gears can be used to increase the turning force (moment) of a bicycle's pedalling motion. Include the role of gear size in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that a smaller front gear (chainring) meshes with a larger rear gear (sprocket). The larger rear gear turns more slowly but with a greater turning effect (torque/moment). This is because moment = force × distance — a larger gear has a larger effective radius. Links to gear ratio: larger gear ÷ smaller gear. Applies to practical situation: riding up a hill requires a high gear ratio for more force; riding on flat at speed requires a lower gear ratio. [5–6 marks]
Secure: Correctly explains that a larger gear produces greater force but turns more slowly, with some reference to gear ratio. [3–4 marks]
Developing: States that gears change speed or force, but lacks explanation linking to moments. [1–2 marks]
Emerging: Minimal physics content. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by nuclear fission.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: the splitting of a large (heavy) nucleus into two smaller nuclei (accept: when a large unstable nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits, releasing energy and more neutrons).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a smoke alarm uses radioactive material to detect smoke.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: the alpha source ionises air in a chamber, creating a small electrical current. 1 mark: smoke particles absorb the alpha radiation, reducing the current and triggering the alarm.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a gamma-emitting isotope with a short half-life, rather than an alpha-emitting isotope with a long half-life, is chosen as a medical tracer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: gamma is chosen because it penetrates the body and can be detected externally (alpha would be absorbed before leaving the body); a short half-life is chosen so the patient is not exposed to radiation for long (once the procedure is done, the source decays quickly to a safe level); an alpha emitter with a long half-life would both fail to escape the body and irradiate internal tissues for a dangerous period. Secure: states gamma penetrates the body for external detection, and short half-life reduces the patient's dose. Developing: states gamma is better without explaining why, or short half-life is safer without reasoning. Emerging: vague reference to penetration or time without linking to the specific requirements.

practice_questions.text: A nuclear power station uses uranium-235 fuel. Describe the process by which energy is released from the fuel and how that energy is used to generate electricity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: uranium-235 nuclei absorb slow-moving neutrons and split (fission), releasing energy and two or three neutrons; control rods absorb excess neutrons to maintain a controlled chain reaction; the energy heats water to produce steam, which drives turbines connected to generators. Secure: describes fission releasing energy that heats water to make steam for turbines, with mention of neutrons and chain reaction. Developing: describes fission and electricity generation but does not mention chain reaction or control. Emerging: mentions nuclear power station producing electricity without describing the process.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following best describes nuclear fusion?
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: Two light nuclei join together to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy. Distractors: A large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei when struck by a neutron; A nucleus releases an alpha particle and two gamma rays; Electrons are accelerated to produce X-rays.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of nuclear fission as an energy source, comparing it with nuclear fusion. Include reference to energy output, waste produced and practical challenges.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: fission — available now in power stations, releases large amounts of energy with no CO₂ emissions during generation, but produces highly radioactive waste requiring thousands of years of safe storage, and carries a small risk of serious accidents; fusion — releases more energy per kilogram of fuel, produces far less long-lived radioactive waste, uses hydrogen isotopes as fuel (abundant), but requires extreme temperatures (tens of millions of degrees) and pressure to initiate, plasma containment remains an engineering challenge, and no commercial fusion plant exists yet; balanced conclusion acknowledging fission is viable now while fusion holds future promise. Secure: addresses energy output, waste and at least one practical challenge for both. Developing: compares fission and fusion with some detail but incomplete or unbalanced. Emerging: describes one process only with minimal comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Which statement correctly describes covalent bonding?
A) Electrons are transferred from a metal to a non-metal
B) A pair of electrons is shared between two non-metal atoms
C) Positive ions are surrounded by delocalised electrons
D) Electrons are transferred from a non-metal to a metal
practice_questions.marks: B) A pair of electrons is shared between two non-metal atoms [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the type of bonding present in a sample of pure copper.
practice_questions.marks: Metallic bonding. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to the electrons when magnesium and oxygen react to form magnesium oxide.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Magnesium loses two electrons to form Mg2+ (cation). Oxygen gains two electrons to form O2- (anion). The oppositely charged ions attract each other.
Secure: Electron transfer described correctly with correct ion charges.
Developing: States that electrons move from magnesium to oxygen but does not give the resulting charges.
Emerging: Vague reference to electrons moving without direction or ion charges.

practice_questions.text: Explain why metals are good conductors of electricity but ionic compounds do not conduct electricity when solid.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Metals have delocalised electrons that are free to move through the structure and carry charge. In ionic compounds the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move, so charge cannot be carried. (Ionic compounds do conduct when molten or dissolved because ions then become free to move.)
Secure: Delocalised electrons in metals linked to conductivity; fixed ions in solid ionic lattice linked to non-conductivity.
Developing: Correct for metals or for ionic compounds but not both.
Emerging: General statement that metals conduct but no explanation linking structure.

practice_questions.text: Aluminium has atomic number 13. Draw the dot-and-cross diagram for aluminium chloride (AlCl3), showing the bonding clearly. State the type of bonding and give the charge on each ion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correct ionic dot-and-cross diagram showing Al3+ in brackets with charge 3+ [1], each Cl- in brackets with charge 1- [1], all outer electrons shown for each ion [1], and correct overall formula AlCl3 with charges balancing to zero [1].
Secure: Three of the four marking points met.
Developing: Diagram drawn but brackets or ion charges missing.
Emerging: Electrons shown but type of bonding or ion charges incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Compare and contrast ionic bonding and covalent bonding. In your answer, describe how each type of bond forms, the particles involved, and give one example of a compound with each type of bonding.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Ionic — electrons transferred from metal to non-metal; forms positive and negative ions; held by electrostatic attraction in a giant lattice; example such as NaCl or MgO. Covalent — electrons shared between non-metal atoms; no charge transfer; molecules or giant structures; example such as H2O, CO2 or Cl2. Clear comparison of similarities (both involve electrostatic forces) and differences (transfer vs sharing; ions vs shared electrons).
Secure: Both types of bonding described accurately with an example each; some comparison made.
Developing: Both described but comparison is limited or one example missing.
Emerging: One type of bonding described only, or significant inaccuracies.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following processes requires energy from respiration?
A) Diffusion
B) Osmosis
C) Active transport
D) All of the above
practice_questions.marks: C) Active transport [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the direction of water movement during osmosis.
practice_questions.marks: Water moves from a dilute solution (high water potential) to a more concentrated solution (low water potential) through a partially permeable membrane. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a student could investigate the effect of sucrose concentration on potato cylinders using osmosis.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for any two of the following:
• Cut potato cylinders of equal size/mass and place each in a different concentration of sucrose solution (1)
• Leave for a set time, blot dry, and measure the change in mass (or length) (1)
• Calculate the percentage change in mass to allow fair comparison (1)
• Repeat to improve reliability / calculate a mean (1)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a single-celled organism such as an amoeba can obtain enough oxygen by diffusion alone, but a mammal cannot.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• A single-celled organism is very small and has a high surface area to volume ratio (1)
• This means diffusion distance to the centre of the cell is short and the rate of diffusion is sufficient to meet the cell's needs (1)
• A mammal is much larger and has a low SA:V ratio — diffusion alone cannot deliver oxygen fast enough to all cells deep inside the organism, so specialised exchange surfaces (e.g. lungs/alveoli) and a circulatory system are needed (1)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A potato cylinder has an initial mass of 4.0 g. After 30 minutes in a sucrose solution, its mass is 3.4 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass and state whether water entered or left the cell. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Percentage change = (change in mass ÷ original mass) × 100 (1)
Change in mass = 3.4 − 4.0 = −0.6 g (1)
Percentage change = (−0.6 ÷ 4.0) × 100 = −15% (1)
Mass decreased, so water left the cell by osmosis — the sucrose solution had a lower water potential than the potato cells (1)
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why root hair cells are well adapted for the absorption of water and mineral ions from the soil.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (up to 6 marks):
• Root hair cells have long, thin extensions that greatly increase the surface area in contact with the soil (1)
• This maximises the rate of absorption by providing more membrane for water and ions to cross (1)
• Water moves into root hair cells by osmosis — from the high water potential of the soil water to the lower water potential inside the cell, through the partially permeable membrane (1)
• Mineral ions are absorbed by active transport against the concentration gradient (1)
• Root hair cells contain many mitochondria to supply the ATP needed for active transport (1)
• The thin cell wall and membrane minimise the diffusion distance for water molecules (1)

StudyVault Mastering: all six points covered with osmosis and active transport distinguished clearly, and SA:V and mitochondria adaptations both named.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following explains why a polythene rod becomes negatively charged when rubbed with a woollen cloth?
A) Positive charges transfer from the cloth to the rod
B) Electrons transfer from the cloth to the rod
C) Protons transfer from the rod to the cloth
D) Electrons transfer from the rod to the cloth
practice_questions.marks:
B) Electrons transfer from the cloth to the rod [1 mark]
Electrons move from the cloth to the rod, giving the rod extra electrons and therefore a negative charge. Protons never transfer; positive charges do not physically move.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by resistance in an electrical circuit.
practice_questions.marks: Resistance is the opposition to the flow of current through a component, measured in ohms (Ω). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A component has a potential difference of 12 V across it and a resistance of 30 Ω.
Calculate the current through the component.
practice_questions.marks:
Identify equation: V = IR, so I = V ÷ R [1 mark]
Substitute: I = 12 ÷ 30 [1 mark]
I = 0.4 A [1 mark]
Unit: A (amperes) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the I-V characteristic of a filament lamp. Explain why the graph has this shape.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes a curve that starts steep and flattens as PD increases (not a straight line). Explains that as more current flows, the filament heats up, increasing resistance. Higher resistance means less current flows for each additional unit of PD, so the graph flattens. [3 marks]
Secure: Correctly describes the shape as a curve and states resistance increases with temperature, but does not link temperature rise to increased current. [2 marks]
Developing: States the graph is a curve but does not explain why. [1 mark]
Emerging: Describes a straight line — incorrect. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A student investigates the resistance of a length of resistance wire. She measures the potential difference across the wire and the current through it at five different settings of a variable resistor. The results give a straight line through the origin on an I-V graph.
Explain what the student can conclude from this result.
practice_questions.marks: The wire is an ohmic conductor [1 mark] because current is directly proportional to potential difference (Ohm's Law holds), which means resistance is constant and temperature has not changed significantly during the experiment [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of a diode and an LDR as components in an automatic night light circuit that switches on when it gets dark. For each component, explain its role and any limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: LDR — resistance increases in the dark, providing a higher voltage signal that can trigger the circuit to switch on. Diode — ensures current flows only in one direction, protecting other components from reverse current damage. Limitations: LDR sensitivity threshold needs calibrating; diode has a forward voltage threshold (~0.6 V for silicon) below which it won't conduct; LDR response time may lag rapidly changing light conditions. Both components are cost-effective and reliable for this application. Justified conclusion on overall suitability. [5–6 marks]
Secure: Correct role for both components, some limitations mentioned. [3–4 marks]
Developing: Correct role for one component only. [1–2 marks]
Emerging: Minimal relevant physics. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT a source of genetic variation in a population?
A) Mutations in DNA
B) Meiosis shuffling chromosomes
C) Sexual reproduction combining alleles from two parents
D) Mitosis producing genetically identical cells
practice_questions.marks: D) Mitosis producing genetically identical cells [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two types of evidence scientists use to support the theory of evolution.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any two from: fossil record / comparative anatomy / DNA analysis / observed examples (e.g. antibiotic resistance, peppered moth) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how geographical isolation can lead to speciation.
practice_questions.marks: A geographical barrier separates a population into two isolated groups [1 mark]; each group evolves separately under different selection pressures until they become so different they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain how antibiotic resistance develops in a population of bacteria. Use the concept of natural selection in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Random mutations give some bacteria resistance to the antibiotic [1 mark]; when the antibiotic is used, resistant bacteria survive and reproduce while non-resistant bacteria are killed [1 mark]; resistant bacteria pass on the resistance allele to offspring, so over time the resistant strain becomes dominant in the population [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A scientist studies a population of dark-coloured and pale-coloured moths living in a woodland. After a period of heavy air pollution that darkened the tree trunks, she records that the proportion of dark moths has increased significantly.
Explain these observations using the theory of natural selection.
practice_questions.marks: Before pollution, pale moths were better camouflaged on pale tree trunks, so dark moths were more visible to predators and eaten more often [1 mark]; after pollution darkened the tree trunks, dark moths became better camouflaged and more likely to survive and reproduce [1 mark]; dark moths passed on the alleles for dark colouring to offspring, so the proportion of dark moths in the population increased over generations [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the evidence for the theory of evolution by natural selection, considering both supporting evidence and historical challenges to the theory's acceptance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed evaluation of at least three types of evidence with specific examples; addresses historical resistance with reasoned explanation; reaches a justified conclusion about strength of evidence.
Secure: Clear explanation of two or more evidence types with examples; some discussion of historical context; conclusion present.
Developing: One or two types of evidence described without full evaluation; limited historical context.
Emerging: Simple list of evidence types without explanation.

Points may include:
Supporting evidence: fossil record shows gradual change; comparative anatomy (pentadactyl limb); DNA analysis shows degree of relatedness; observable examples within human timescales (antibiotic resistance, peppered moth).
Historical challenges: contradicted prevailing religious explanations for creation; insufficient fossil record at the time (gaps now largely filled); genetics not yet understood in Darwin's era (Mendel's work on heredity was not linked to Darwin's theory until the modern synthesis of the 20th century).
Conclusion should weigh strength of evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct formula for percentage yield?
A) (Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all products) × 100
B) (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100
C) (theoretical yield ÷ actual yield) × 100
D) (actual yield ÷ Mr of desired product) × 100
practice_questions.marks: B) (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) State one advantage and one disadvantage of bioleaching compared to traditional smelting.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of: Advantage — e.g. requires less energy / can extract metal from low-grade ores that are uneconomical to smelt / lower environmental impact from land disturbance. Disadvantage — e.g. the process is very slow / produces acidic leachate that must be managed carefully / yield per unit time is lower than smelting. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain how phytomining is used to extract copper from low-grade ore.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Plants (hyperaccumulators) absorb copper ions from the soil through their roots and accumulate them in their tissues; the plants are then harvested and burned; the resulting ash contains a concentrated copper compound which is processed to extract the copper. All three stages described correctly with accurate scientific language.
Secure: Two of the three stages described correctly with mostly accurate language.
Developing: One stage described with some accuracy; limited chemical detail.
Emerging: A general statement about using plants; no process detail. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A reaction to produce calcium oxide has a theoretical yield of 56 g. Only 42 g is actually obtained. Calculate the percentage yield. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Correct formula (1): percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100. Correct substitution (1): (42 ÷ 56) × 100. Correct answer (1): 75%. Correct unit or confirmation that percentage requires no unit (1). [4 marks — common error: dividing theoretical by actual instead of actual by theoretical]

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer produces a polymer by reacting two monomers. The only product is the desired polymer. Explain why the atom economy for this reaction is 100%, and explain why the percentage yield might still be less than 100%.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Atom economy is 100% because all the reactant atoms end up in the single product (no by-products are formed in the balanced equation); percentage yield can still be below 100% because the reaction may be incomplete, product may be lost during processing, or a reversible reaction may not go fully to completion.
Secure: Both concepts distinguished with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: One concept explained correctly; the other confused or missing.
Emerging: States that both measures relate to yield without distinguishing them. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Life cycle assessments always give an objective picture of a product's environmental impact.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Thorough explanation that LCAs cover all four stages (raw materials, manufacture, use, disposal) and consider multiple environmental factors (energy, emissions, water, waste); however they involve subjective weighting of different factors, and data may be incomplete or selectively reported by companies for marketing purposes. A balanced conclusion reached.
Secure: LCAs explained with two or more stages covered; one or two limitations discussed; conclusion present.
Developing: LCAs described at a basic level; limited or no discussion of subjectivity.
Emerging: A general statement about LCAs with little accurate detail. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: State the equation for gravitational potential energy and identify the unit of each quantity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: GPE = m × g × h; m in kg, g in N/kg, h in metres, GPE in joules.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to the energy stored in a compressed spring when it is released and propels a ball upwards.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: elastic potential energy in the spring is transferred to kinetic energy of the ball as it is released. 1 mark: as the ball rises, kinetic energy is transferred to gravitational potential energy (some is also dissipated as thermal energy due to air resistance).

practice_questions.text: A cyclist of total mass 70 kg (including the bicycle) travels at 8 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy of the cyclist. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct equation KE = ½ × m × v². 1 mark: correct substitution KE = ½ × 70 × 8². 1 mark: v² = 64 correctly evaluated, giving KE = ½ × 70 × 64 = 2240. 1 mark: correct answer 2240 J with correct unit.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a car travelling at 30 m/s requires a much greater braking distance than the same car travelling at 15 m/s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: states that KE = ½mv² so KE depends on v²; the car at 30 m/s has four times the KE of the car at 15 m/s (since speed is doubled, KE is quadrupled); braking force is constant so the car must travel four times the distance to dissipate four times the KE. Secure: states doubling speed quadruples KE and therefore quadruples braking distance. Developing: states higher speed means more KE and longer braking distance without using the v² relationship. Emerging: simply states faster speed means harder to stop, no reference to KE.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following is the correct unit for power?
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: Watts (W). Distractors: Joules (J); Newtons (N); Joules per metre (J/m).

practice_questions.text: An electric motor lifts a 150 N load through a height of 3 m in 5 seconds. The motor uses 1200 J of electrical energy during this time. Calculate the efficiency of the motor and evaluate one way in which the wasted energy could be reduced.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: calculates useful work done = 150 × 3 = 450 J; calculates efficiency = 450 ÷ 1200 = 0.375 = 37.5%; identifies that wasted energy is likely heat due to friction in the motor; suggests lubrication to reduce friction and improve efficiency; recognises 62.5% of input energy is wasted and evaluates whether improving efficiency is worthwhile. Secure: correct efficiency calculation with one improvement method identified. Developing: calculates useful work correctly but makes an error in efficiency equation, or efficiency is correct but no evaluation of improvement. Emerging: identifies useful output and input energy but cannot calculate efficiency correctly.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes phloem tissue?
A) Dead cells reinforced with lignin that transport water upwards
B) Living cells with sieve plates that transport sucrose up and down
C) Dead cells that transport mineral ions by active transport
D) Living cells that carry oxygen-rich blood to tissues
practice_questions.marks: B) Living cells with sieve plates that transport sucrose up and down [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two features of alveoli that make them efficient gas exchange surfaces.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the following (1 mark for any two correct):
• Large total surface area
• Thin walls (one cell thick) to minimise diffusion distance
• Moist inner surface to allow gases to dissolve
• Rich capillary network to maintain steep concentration gradients
[1 mark for two correct features]

practice_questions.text: Describe two differences between arteries and veins.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for any two of the following:
• Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood back to the heart (1)
• Arteries have thicker, more muscular and elastic walls than veins (1)
• Arteries carry blood at high pressure; veins carry blood at low pressure (1)
• Veins contain valves to prevent backflow; arteries do not (1)
• Arteries have a smaller lumen; veins have a larger lumen (1)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how xylem vessels are adapted for transporting water from the roots to the leaves.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Xylem cells are dead and hollow, forming continuous tubes for water to flow through with little resistance (1)
• The walls are reinforced with lignin, which is waterproof and rigid — preventing the vessels from collapsing under the tension created by the transpiration stream (1)
• Water is drawn upwards continuously as it evaporates from the leaves through stomata (the transpiration stream), creating a 'pull' / cohesion-tension that maintains the water column (1)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: In bright sunlight, the transpiration rate of a plant is measured as 3.6 cm³ of water lost per hour. When a fan is added to increase air movement, the rate increases to 5.4 cm³ per hour. Calculate the percentage increase in transpiration rate. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Percentage increase = (change ÷ original) × 100 (1)
Change = 5.4 − 3.6 = 1.8 cm³/hour (1)
Percentage increase = (1.8 ÷ 3.6) × 100 (1)
= 50% (1)
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare how substances are transported in plants and in humans. Include reference to the structures involved and the mechanisms used.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (up to 6 marks):
• In plants, xylem transports water and minerals upwards from roots to leaves by the transpiration stream — passive process driven by evaporation (1)
• Phloem transports sucrose (from photosynthesis) up and down the plant by translocation — requires energy (active process) (1)
• In humans, the double circulatory system uses the heart to pump blood — right side to lungs, left side to body (1)
• Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; veins return blood at low pressure using valves to prevent backflow; capillaries allow exchange with tissues (1)
• Blood plasma transports dissolved glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones and CO₂; red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin (1)
• Both plant and human systems use exchange surfaces with large surface area, thin walls and good supply of the transport medium to maximise diffusion rates (alveoli/villi in humans; root hair cells/stomata in plants) (1)

StudyVault Mastering: plant and human transport both covered in detail, with mechanisms (passive/active) distinguished and structural adaptations linked to function.

practice_questions.text:
Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
A) Graphite has ionic bonds but diamond has covalent bonds
B) Graphite has delocalised electrons that can move freely, but diamond uses all outer electrons in covalent bonds
C) Diamond has a higher melting point than graphite
D) Graphite has a giant structure but diamond is a simple molecule
practice_questions.marks: B) Graphite has delocalised electrons that can move freely, but diamond uses all outer electrons in covalent bonds [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the size range (in nanometres) of a nanoparticle.
practice_questions.marks: Roughly 1 to 100 nm (nanometres). Accept answers specifying approximately this range. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of graphite and explain why it is used as a lubricant.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Graphite has flat hexagonal layers of carbon atoms. The layers are held by weak intermolecular forces and can slide over each other easily, making it useful as a lubricant.
Secure: Identifies layered structure and explains sliding.
Developing: Mentions layers but does not link to sliding/lubricant property.
Emerging: Vague description of graphite structure without explaining the lubricant property.

practice_questions.text: Explain why ionic compounds have high melting points but simple molecular compounds have low melting points.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Ionic compounds have strong electrostatic forces of attraction between many oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice. A large amount of energy is needed to break all these forces. Simple molecular compounds have weak intermolecular forces between small molecules; little energy is needed to overcome these, so they melt at low temperatures. The strong covalent bonds within the molecules are not broken on melting.
Secure: Both types explained with reference to the forces broken during melting.
Developing: Correct for one type only; the other is incomplete or refers to breaking covalent bonds for simple molecules.
Emerging: States that one has a high melting point and the other a low one without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Titanium dioxide nanoparticles are used in sunscreen. The surface area of 1 g of titanium dioxide nanoparticles is much greater than 1 g of bulk titanium dioxide powder. Explain why the large surface area to volume ratio makes nanoparticles more effective in sunscreen.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Large surface area to volume ratio means a greater proportion of the atoms are on the surface and available to interact with UV radiation [1]. This means nanoparticles absorb or scatter UV more effectively per gram than bulk powder [1]. Nanoparticles are small enough to be transparent to visible light so sunscreen appears colourless [1]. Overall, less material is needed to achieve the same UV protection, making nanoparticle sunscreens more efficient [1].
Secure: Surface area to volume ratio linked to greater UV interaction and transparency; three of four marking points.
Developing: Mentions large surface area but explanation of effectiveness is incomplete.
Emerging: States nanoparticles are smaller without explaining why this improves performance.

practice_questions.text: Silver nanoparticles are added to some wound dressings to reduce infection. Evaluate the use of silver nanoparticles in medical applications, considering both the benefits and possible risks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Benefits: silver at nanoscale has greater antibacterial activity per gram (large surface area to volume ratio allows more atoms to interact with bacteria); effective against a broad range of bacteria; may reduce reliance on antibiotics. Risks: nanoparticles are small enough to enter cells and tissues; long-term health effects not fully understood; potential for environmental accumulation if silver nanoparticles are washed into water systems; antibacterial resistance to silver is a concern. Conclusion: balances the medical benefits (reduced infection, faster healing) against genuine scientific uncertainty about long-term effects, arguing that continued research and risk monitoring are important.
Secure: At least two benefits and two risks given; some evaluation reaching a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Benefits and risks listed but evaluation is limited.
Emerging: Only benefits or only risks discussed, with no balanced evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following statements about transformers is correct?
A) Transformers work with both alternating and direct current
B) A step-up transformer increases voltage and current simultaneously
C) The secondary voltage depends on the ratio of turns in the two coils
D) Transformers create electrical energy from mechanical energy
practice_questions.marks: C) The secondary voltage depends on the ratio of turns in the two coils [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the equation that links the voltages and number of turns in a transformer.
practice_questions.marks: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns [1 mark — accept equivalent forms]

practice_questions.text: Describe why the National Grid transmits electrical power at a high voltage rather than a low voltage.
practice_questions.marks: High voltage means a lower current in the cables (1). Lower current means less power is lost as heat in the cables / power loss = I²R so lower I means less loss (1). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a transformer works. In your answer, include the role of alternating current and the iron core.
practice_questions.marks: An alternating current in the primary coil creates an alternating/changing magnetic field (1). The iron core carries/concentrates this changing magnetic field to the secondary coil (1). The changing magnetic field in the secondary coil induces an alternating potential difference / voltage across it (1). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A transformer at a power station has 200 turns on the primary coil and 40 000 turns on the secondary coil. The primary voltage is 25 000 V and the primary current is 500 A.
(a) Calculate the secondary voltage.
(b) Calculate the secondary current, assuming an ideal transformer.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Vp / Vs = Np / Ns → Vs = Vp × (Ns / Np) = 25 000 × (40 000 / 200) = 25 000 × 200 = 5 000 000 V (or 5 MV) [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for correct answer with unit]
(b) Vp × Ip = Vs × Is → Is = (Vp × Ip) / Vs = (25 000 × 500) / 5 000 000 = 12 500 000 / 5 000 000 = 2.5 A [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for correct answer with unit] [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that 'transformers are perfectly efficient devices.' In your answer, discuss the principle of energy conservation in an ideal transformer, the equation Vp × Ip = Vs × Is, and the reasons why real transformers lose a small amount of energy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): States that in an ideal transformer, energy is conserved — all power input equals power output, giving Vp × Ip = Vs × Is. Explains that if voltage is stepped up, current is stepped down proportionally so power remains constant. Acknowledges that real transformers are not perfectly efficient — energy is lost as heat in the resistance of the coils, and as 'eddy currents' induced in the iron core (candidates do not need to use the term 'eddy currents' but should reference heat losses in the core or coil). Concludes that while very close to ideal (modern large transformers are typically over 99% efficient), real transformers do lose some energy. Awarded top band only if the candidate uses correct physics throughout and reaches a justified conclusion about the extent to which the claim is valid.
Secure (3–4 marks): Correctly states energy conservation in ideal transformer and the power equation. Notes that real transformers have some losses but may not explain the mechanism fully.
Developing (1–2 marks): Recognises that power in equals power out for ideal case, or mentions real losses, but treatment is incomplete. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Name the type of neurone that carries impulses from the CNS to an effector.
practice_questions.marks: Motor neurone. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens at a synapse when a nerve impulse reaches the end of a neurone.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Neurotransmitters are released from vesicles into the synaptic cleft (1); they diffuse across the gap and bind to specific receptor molecules on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse (1). Emerging: Vague reference to 'chemicals crossing the gap' without naming neurotransmitters or explaining receptor binding.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a reflex response is faster than a voluntary response to the same stimulus.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The reflex arc passes through the spinal cord rather than the brain (1), so the pathway is shorter with fewer synapses to cross (1), meaning the impulse reaches the effector more quickly (1). Secure: Two of the three points clearly linked. Developing: States reflexes are faster but gives no mechanistic explanation. Emerging: Vague or incorrect — e.g. 'the muscles react on their own'.

practice_questions.text: A student holds a ruler vertically and releases it unexpectedly. The subject's hand moves 0.12 m before catching it. Use the equation t = √(2d ÷ g), where d is the distance fallen in metres and g = 9.8 m/s², to calculate the reaction time. Show your working and give your answer to 2 significant figures.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Substitution correct — t = √(2 × 0.12 ÷ 9.8) (1); correct calculation of 0.24 ÷ 9.8 = 0.02449 (1); square root taken correctly: t = 0.156 s (1); rounded correctly to 2 s.f.: 0.16 s with unit (1). Penalise missing unit or incorrect rounding.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the eye focuses on a nearby object. In your answer, refer to the ciliary muscles, suspensory ligaments and the lens.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Ciliary muscles contract (1); suspensory ligaments slacken/go slack (1); lens becomes fatter/more curved, increasing refraction to focus light on the retina (1). Secure: Two points with correct logic. Developing: States 'lens changes shape' but does not describe the mechanism. Emerging: Confused — e.g. 'muscles relax so lens gets fatter'.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using reflex actions to protect the body. In your answer, consider speed of response, level of control and potential limitations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Reflexes are very rapid because they bypass the brain and use only spinal cord relay neurones, reducing the number of synapses crossed; this is advantageous in situations of immediate danger (touching heat, sharp objects). Reflexes are involuntary — they cannot be easily overridden, which ensures a consistent protective response. However, the lack of conscious control can be a disadvantage: the response is fixed and cannot be modified based on context. Voluntary responses, though slower, allow the organism to assess danger and make a considered decision. A well-argued conclusion noting that reflexes are essential for survival but limited in scope. Secure: Four well-reasoned points. Developing: Two points with limited evaluation. Emerging: One point with no evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct general formula for alkanes?
A) CnH2n
B) CnH2n+1
C) CnH2n+2
D) CnH2n-2
practice_questions.marks: C) CnH2n+2 [1 mark — common error: writing CnH2n which is the formula for alkenes]

practice_questions.text: State the conditions needed for the fermentation of glucose to ethanol.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: yeast / anaerobic conditions (absence of oxygen) / temperature of approximately 25–35 °C. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why bromine water can be used to distinguish between an alkane and an alkene.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Alkenes contain a C=C double bond; bromine adds across this double bond in an addition reaction, decolourising the orange bromine water to colourless. Alkanes are saturated (no double bond) so cannot react with bromine water in this way, leaving the solution orange.
Secure: Correct observation stated (decolourisation with alkene, no change with alkane) and one explanation given.
Developing: Correct observation only, no explanation of the double bond.
Emerging: Partial observation with no chemical explanation. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A student carries out cracking and obtains decane (C10H22) and ethene (C2H4) from a longer-chain alkane. Calculate the molecular formula of the original alkane that was cracked.
practice_questions.marks: Identifying that cracking splits one molecule into two (1). Writing the formula of the starting material by adding decane and ethene: C10H22 + C2H4 = C12H26 (1). Confirming the formula fits the alkane general formula CnH2n+2 where n=12: C12H2(12)+2 = C12H26 ✓ (1). Correct answer stated clearly: dodecane, C12H26 (1). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain the difference between addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation. In your answer, refer to the types of monomers used and the products formed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addition polymerisation uses monomers containing a C=C double bond (alkenes); the double bond opens and monomers join — no other product is formed (100% atom economy). Condensation polymerisation uses monomers with two functional groups (e.g. diols and dicarboxylic acids); bonds form at both ends of each monomer with elimination of a small molecule (usually water) at each bond formed.
Secure: Both types described with at least two correct distinguishing features.
Developing: One type described correctly; the other partially or incorrectly described.
Emerging: A general statement that both involve monomers joining, with no distinguishing detail. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Fermentation is a more sustainable way to produce ethanol than hydration of ethene.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Fermentation uses plant sugars as a renewable feedstock, produces ethanol at low temperatures and pressures using minimal energy, and carbon dioxide released is offset by that absorbed by growing the crops (lower net carbon footprint); however the process is slow, produces dilute ethanol requiring further purification, and fermentation efficiency depends on crop growing conditions. Hydration uses ethene from cracking crude oil (finite resource), requires higher temperatures and pressures (more energy), but produces higher-purity ethanol more quickly. Balanced conclusion reached.
Secure: At least two advantages of fermentation and one disadvantage discussed; hydration compared; conclusion present.
Developing: One or two points about fermentation; limited comparison with hydration.
Emerging: General claim that fermentation is renewable with no further analysis. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is true about components connected in parallel?
A) They share the same current
B) They share the same potential difference
C) The total resistance increases as more components are added
D) The circuit stops working if one component fails
practice_questions.marks:
B) They share the same potential difference [1 mark]
In a parallel circuit, each branch has the same PD (the supply voltage). Current is shared between branches. Adding components in parallel decreases total resistance. A single branch failing does not stop others.

practice_questions.text: State the UK mains supply voltage and frequency.
practice_questions.marks:
230 V and 50 Hz [1 mark]
(Both values required for the mark)

practice_questions.text:
A kettle has a power rating of 2 200 W. It is connected to the 230 V mains supply.
Calculate the current drawn by the kettle. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
practice_questions.marks:
Identify equation: P = VI, so I = P ÷ V [1 mark]
Substitute: I = 2200 ÷ 230 [1 mark]
I = 9.565… ≈ 9.6 A (2 s.f.) [1 mark]
Unit: A (amperes) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain why electricity is transmitted through the National Grid at high voltage and low current, rather than at low voltage and high current. Refer to a relevant equation in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that cables have resistance. Uses P = I²R to show that power wasted as heat depends on current squared — so a smaller current dramatically reduces power losses. High voltage achieves the same power transfer at lower current (P = VI). [3 marks]
Secure: States high voltage gives low current and mentions reduced energy losses, but does not reference the equation. [2 marks]
Developing: States 'high voltage is more efficient' without further explanation. [1 mark]
Emerging: Vague or incorrect. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the earth wire and the fuse in a three-pin plug as a combined safety system. Include what happens if the live wire contacts the metal casing of an appliance.
practice_questions.marks: If the live wire contacts the metal casing, a large current surges through the earth wire to ground [1 mark]. This large current exceeds the fuse rating, causing the fuse wire to melt and break the live wire connection, cutting off the supply and preventing electrocution or fire [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
A student uses a 60 W laptop for 3 hours per day for 30 days. Electricity costs 28p per kWh.
Calculate the total cost of running the laptop over 30 days. Show all steps.
practice_questions.marks:
Power in kW: 60 W = 0.06 kW [1 mark]
Time: 3 h/day × 30 days = 90 h [1 mark]
Energy = 0.06 × 90 = 5.4 kWh [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for value]
Cost = 5.4 × 28 = 151.2p = £1.51 [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for correct answer with unit]

Mastering: All steps shown, correct answer in pence or pounds.
Secure: Correct method; minor arithmetic error.
Developing: Converts W to kW or calculates energy but not cost.
Emerging: Uses kW and hours but does not complete the calculation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following equations is correctly balanced?
A) Na + Cl2 → NaCl
B) 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl
C) Na + 2Cl → NaCl2
D) 2Na + Cl2 → NaCl2
practice_questions.marks: B) 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what the state symbol (aq) means in a chemical equation.
practice_questions.marks: Dissolved in water / in aqueous solution. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: When magnesium ribbon burns in air, white magnesium oxide powder is formed. The mass of the product is greater than the mass of the magnesium ribbon used. Describe why the product is heavier and explain how this is consistent with conservation of mass.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Magnesium reacts with oxygen from the air to form magnesium oxide. The oxygen atoms from the air are incorporated into the product, increasing the mass. The total mass of all reactants (magnesium + oxygen) equals the total mass of the product magnesium oxide, consistent with conservation of mass.
Secure: Identifies oxygen from air is added and links to conservation of mass.
Developing: States that oxygen is added but does not explain conservation of mass.
Emerging: States that the product is heavier without explaining why.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by conservation of mass in a chemical reaction, and describe how you could demonstrate it experimentally.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Conservation of mass means the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products because atoms are rearranged but not created or destroyed. To demonstrate: carry out a reaction in a sealed container (e.g. reacting sodium hydroxide solution with hydrochloric acid in a sealed flask), measure the mass before and after, and show it is the same. The sealed container ensures no gas escapes.
Secure: Defines conservation of mass and describes a suitable method with a sealed container.
Developing: Defines conservation of mass correctly but description of experiment is incomplete.
Emerging: States that mass is conserved but explanation is vague.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of ammonium sulfate, (NH4)2SO4. (Relative atomic masses: N = 14, H = 1, S = 32, O = 16.) Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies atoms: 2N, 8H, 1S, 4O [1]. Calculates: (2 × 14) + (8 × 1) + 32 + (4 × 16) = 28 + 8 + 32 + 64 [1]. Total Mr = 132 [1]. Working clearly shown with correct arithmetic [1].
Secure: Correct answer of 132 with method shown; 3 of 4 marking points met.
Developing: Method correct but arithmetic error in final step.
Emerging: Some atom counts correct but formula not correctly interpreted (e.g. counts only 4 H not 8).

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Iron reacts with hydrochloric acid according to the equation: Fe(s) + 2HCl(aq) → FeCl2(aq) + H2(g). Calculate the mass of iron chloride (FeCl2) produced when 5.6 g of iron reacts completely with excess hydrochloric acid. (Relative atomic masses: Fe = 56, Cl = 35.5.) Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mr of FeCl2 = 56 + (2 × 35.5) = 127 [1]. Moles of Fe = 5.6 ÷ 56 = 0.1 mol [1]. From the equation, 1 mol Fe forms 1 mol FeCl2, so moles of FeCl2 = 0.1 mol [1]. Mass of FeCl2 = 0.1 × 127 = 12.7 g [1]. Units included throughout [1]. Conservation of mass check: 5.6 g Fe + 7.3 g HCl (from 0.2 mol × 36.5) = 12.9 g; minus 0.2 g H2 (from 0.1 mol × 2) = 12.7 g FeCl2 ✓ [1].
Secure: Correct moles and mass calculated with working; 4 of 6 marking points.
Developing: Correct moles of Fe calculated but mole ratio or final mass incorrect.
Emerging: Mr calculated correctly but moles not used correctly in subsequent steps.

practice_questions.text:
A scientist uses capture-recapture to estimate the population of water voles in a wetland. She catches and marks 48 voles, then releases them. Two weeks later she catches 36 voles, of which 9 are marked.
Calculate the estimated population of water voles. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: N = (n₁ × n₂) ÷ m₂ [1 mark]
Substitution: N = (48 × 36) ÷ 9 [1 mark]
Calculation: N = 1728 ÷ 9 [1 mark]
Answer: N = 192 water voles [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an indicator species for clean, well-oxygenated freshwater?
A) Rat-tailed maggot
B) Bloodworm
C) Stonefly nymph
D) Sludgeworm
practice_questions.marks: C) Stonefly nymph [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two assumptions that must hold for a capture-recapture estimate to be reliable.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two from: marked individuals must mix randomly back into the population [1 mark]; marking must not affect survival or behaviour [1 mark]; no significant births, deaths, immigration or emigration between the two samples [1 mark]
(2 marks total — 1 mark per valid assumption)

practice_questions.text: Explain how eutrophication causes a decrease in the number of fish in a lake. Include the role of decomposing bacteria in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Fertiliser run-off causes rapid algal growth (algal bloom) which blocks sunlight, killing aquatic plants [1 mark]; when the algae die, decomposing bacteria multiply rapidly and use up dissolved oxygen in the water through aerobic respiration [1 mark]; oxygen levels fall so low that fish and other aerobic organisms cannot survive and suffocate/die [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name one indicator species and state how it is used to assess the level of air pollution in an area.
practice_questions.marks:
Lichens [1 mark] — the presence of bushy/leafy lichens indicates clean air; their absence (or presence of only crusty lichens) indicates air pollution
Accept: any correctly named air pollution indicator species with an accurate description of how it indicates pollution level

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of maintaining high biodiversity in ecosystems, considering both ecological and human perspectives.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion with developed ecological and human arguments; specific examples used; justified conclusion.
Secure: Clear arguments from at least two perspectives; some development with examples; conclusion present.
Developing: Points made but not fully developed; limited perspective range.
Emerging: Simple statements with little development or examples.

Points may include:
Ecological: stable ecosystems need many species filling different roles; loss of one species can trigger cascade effects (e.g. loss of pollinators reduces plant reproduction); higher biodiversity increases ecosystem resilience to change.
Human: medicines derived from natural organisms (many pharmaceuticals originate from plant or microbial compounds); food security depends on diversity of crops and pollinators; ecotourism economic value; moral/ethical responsibility to protect life on Earth.
Conclusion should weigh the evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a renewable energy source?
A) Coal
B) Natural gas
C) Nuclear fuel
D) Wind
practice_questions.marks: D) Wind [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using solar panels to generate electricity.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct point (max 2):
Advantage: any one of — produces no CO2 during operation / no fuel cost / sustainable / does not run out.
